title: From Frozen Ponds to Factories: The Making of Artificial Cold
paras: A

For most of human history, keeping food cold depended entirely on nature. In Persia, China and parts of Europe, wealthy families built ice houses: deep, well-insulated pits or buildings where ice and snow collected in winter were packed in straw. With care, the ice could last until late summer, cooling drinks and preserving fish and meat for those who could afford it. For ordinary people, however, cold was seasonal and unpredictable. Food was preserved by drying, salting or smoking, methods that changed its taste and did not suit fresh produce such as milk.
B

The idea that cold could be sold in large quantities belongs largely to a young Boston merchant, Frederic Tudor. In 1806 he sent a ship loaded with ice cut from New England ponds to the Caribbean island of Martinique. Many observers considered the plan ridiculous, and they were partly right: much of the cargo melted, few people on the island knew what to do with the rest, and Tudor lost money. He persisted nonetheless. Over the following years he experimented with insulation, eventually settling on sawdust, a waste product of the region's timber mills, and he built storage houses at the ports he supplied. By the 1830s, ice from Massachusetts was being unloaded in Calcutta after a voyage of four months.
C

As demand grew, ice harvesting became an industry in its own right. In 1825 Nathaniel Wyeth, one of Tudor's suppliers, introduced a horse-drawn cutter that scored the frozen surface of a lake in a grid, so that workers could saw out blocks of identical size. Regular blocks could be stacked tightly, leaving fewer air gaps, and therefore melted more slowly. Yet the trade remained at the mercy of the weather. A mild winter meant thin ice, a poor harvest and a sharp rise in prices the following summer. There was also a growing problem of quality: lakes near expanding cities were often polluted, and doctors began to warn that natural ice could carry disease.
D

Meanwhile, scientists had begun to understand how cold might be manufactured. In the middle of the eighteenth century, the Scottish professor William Cullen showed his students at the University of Glasgow that when a liquid evaporates rapidly it absorbs heat from its surroundings; by lowering the pressure over a container of ether, he produced a small quantity of ice. Cullen regarded this as a scientific curiosity rather than a practical invention. Almost eighty years later, the American inventor Jacob Perkins, then working in London, patented a machine in which the evaporated fluid was compressed and turned back into a liquid, so that it could be used again and again in a closed cycle. This principle, known as vapour compression, still underlies most refrigerators today, but Perkins's machine never became a commercial success.
E

Practical ice-making owed much to people working far from the great scientific centres. John Gorrie, a doctor in the small port of Apalachicola, Florida, wanted to cool the rooms of patients suffering from fever. The machine he built for this purpose also produced ice, and he received a patent for it in 1851. Gorrie, however, could not find investors, and some newspapers mocked the very notion of man-made ice. In Australia, James Harrison, a Scottish-born printer living in Geelong, noticed that the ether he used to clean metal type made the metal feel extremely cold. In the 1850s he built ice machines and supplied cooling equipment to a local brewery. His ambition to send frozen meat to Britain ended in disappointment, however, when an attempt in 1873 failed and the cargo spoiled on the voyage.
F

The breakthrough came from the brewing industry. Lager beer must be fermented and stored at low temperatures, which restricted production to the colder months unless large amounts of natural ice were available. In the 1870s the German engineer Carl von Linde, whose research was funded partly by a brewery in Munich, designed a compression machine using ammonia that was far more efficient and reliable than earlier models. Breweries across Europe soon adopted his design. Refrigerated shipping followed: in 1882 the sailing ship Dunedin arrived in London with a cargo of frozen lamb from New Zealand in good condition, opening a trade that would transform farming in the southern hemisphere.
G

Electric refrigerators for the home began to appear in the 1910s, though they were expensive, and many early models used toxic gases such as ammonia or sulphur dioxide, which occasionally leaked with fatal results. Around 1930, chemists developed chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), which were neither poisonous nor flammable and were welcomed as a perfect solution. Only decades later was it discovered that CFCs released into the atmosphere were damaging the ozone layer, and in 1987 the Montreal Protocol began their gradual removal. The history of refrigeration, in other words, is not a simple story of progress: each answer to the problem of cold has eventually raised new questions of its own.

title: The Great Good Place: Why Communities Need Third Places
paras: A

In 1989 the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg published a book with an unusual subject: the ordinary places where people meet when they are neither at home nor at work. Oldenburg called the home the 'first place' and the workplace the 'second place'. Cafés, pubs, barbers' shops, community centres and the steps of a busy library were, in his terms, 'third places'. He argued that such places were essential to a healthy society, and he was alarmed by what he saw as their disappearance from much of the United States. More than three decades later, his term has entered the vocabulary of urban planners, architects and even coffee-shop chains, though not always with the meaning he intended.
B

Oldenburg was careful to say that not every public venue qualifies. A true third place, he wrote, is neutral ground: nobody is obliged to be there and nobody plays the role of host, so people can come and go as they please. It acts as a leveller, meaning that a person's income or job title counts for little once they are inside. Conversation is the main activity, and it tends to be playful rather than serious. Such places are usually plain and unpretentious in appearance, and their character comes less from the furniture than from the regulars, the small group of customers who are there most days and who make newcomers feel either welcome or out of place.
C

Why should any of this matter? Part of the answer lies in an influential 1973 paper by the sociologist Mark Granovetter, who studied how people found new jobs. Surprisingly, the most useful contacts were not close friends but acquaintances, people seen only occasionally. Close friends tend to know the same things we do; acquaintances move in other circles and so can pass on information we would not otherwise hear. Granovetter called this 'the strength of weak ties'. Third places are where weak ties are formed and maintained, almost without effort. They also offer something harder to measure: a sense, especially valuable for older people who live alone, of being recognised, and of being missed when absent.
D

If third places are so useful, why did Oldenburg believe they were vanishing? He pointed first to the design of post-war suburbs. Zoning laws in many American towns kept housing strictly separate from shops and businesses, so that residents had to drive to reach anywhere at all, and a casual stop on the way home became impractical. Longer commutes left less free time. Commercial pressures played a part too. Many chain restaurants and cafés are designed for rapid turnover: bright lighting, loud music and seats that become uncomfortable after half an hour all encourage customers to leave once they have paid, which is the opposite of what a third place requires.
E

Some researchers have suggested that the internet now performs the function that the corner café once did. In a 2006 study, Constance Steinkuehler and Dmitri Williams argued that large online multiplayer games met many of Oldenburg's criteria: players gathered voluntarily, status in the outside world was invisible, and conversation flowed freely. Critics accept that online communities can be valuable but doubt that they are equivalent. Physical places bring together people who would never choose each other's company, whereas online platforms often sort users into groups of like-minded people, which undermines the levelling effect that Oldenburg considered so important.
F

Whatever the role of the internet, there have been deliberate attempts to restore physical third places. Many public libraries have been redesigned with cafés, comfortable seating and maker spaces, where people can share tools and equipment. In 2010 San Francisco began allowing businesses and residents to convert parking spaces into 'parklets', small public seating areas on the edge of the pavement, and the idea has since spread to cities on several continents. Planners increasingly favour mixed-use developments in which flats are built above shops, partly in the hope of making the casual encounter possible again.
G

Not everyone, however, shares the enthusiasm for third places. Oldenburg's descriptions, some critics argue, are coloured by nostalgia for a kind of tavern or barber's shop that was never as welcoming as he suggested; women and minority groups were often excluded from such places in practice. Even today, a café is open only to those who can afford to buy something, and a group of loyal regulars can make outsiders feel unwelcome. There is also the risk that fashionable new cafés, opened in the name of community, push up rents and force out the older, cheaper venues where long-standing residents used to meet. A third place for one group may be a closed door for another.

title: The Words We Think In
paras: A

It is a claim that appears regularly in popular articles: a language that lacks a word for something prevents its speakers from thinking about it. In its strongest form, this idea, known as linguistic determinism, holds that the language we happen to learn as children sets the limits of what we can understand. The strong version is almost certainly false. People invent new words whenever they need them; translation between languages, though imperfect, is always possible; and infants reason about objects and quantities before they can speak at all. Yet the rejection of determinism has too often been treated as the end of the matter. A weaker claim, that the language we speak influences how we habitually think, is far more plausible, and it deserves a more careful hearing than its critics have generally given it.
B

The idea is most closely associated with Benjamin Lee Whorf, an American chemical engineer who worked for a fire insurance company and studied linguistics in his spare time. As an inspector, Whorf noticed that workers who behaved cautiously around full petrol drums became careless near drums described as 'empty', smoking beside them even though these contained explosive vapour. The word, he concluded, had shaped their perception of danger. Whorf went on to make much bolder claims, most famously that the Hopi language of Arizona contained no words or grammatical forms referring to time as something that could be counted or divided, and that the Hopi therefore experienced time quite differently from Europeans.
C

Whorf's Hopi claims did not survive scrutiny. In 1983 the linguist Ekkehart Malotki published a detailed study documenting the many ways in which Hopi speakers refer to time, including units such as days and seasons and devices that function much like tense. By then, the intellectual climate had changed. Linguists influenced by the search for a universal grammar shared by all humans were inclined to see differences between languages as superficial, and linguistic relativity came to be regarded as a discredited fashion. In my view, this reaction went too far. That Whorf was wrong about the Hopi tells us that he was careless with evidence, not that the question he raised was meaningless.
D

Some of the most persuasive evidence for a weaker form of relativity concerns colour. Russian, unlike English, has two basic words for blue: 'goluboy' for lighter shades and 'siniy' for darker ones, and speakers must choose between them. In a 2007 study, Jonathan Winawer and his colleagues showed Russian and English speakers sets of blue squares and asked them to identify which two matched. Russian speakers were faster when the shades fell on opposite sides of their language's boundary, while English speakers showed no such advantage. Crucially, the Russian advantage disappeared when participants were asked to rehearse a string of numbers silently during the task, which kept the verbal parts of their minds occupied. This suggests that language was not permanently reshaping what they saw; rather, it was being called upon in the moment to help them sort what they saw.
E

Spatial thinking provides a more dramatic case. Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northern Queensland, rarely use words such as 'left' and 'right'; instead, they describe locations in terms of compass directions, saying, for example, that a cup is to the north of a plate. Researchers led by Stephen Levinson found that when such speakers were shown objects arranged on a table, turned through 180 degrees and asked to reproduce the arrangement, they preserved the compass directions rather than the order relative to their own bodies. Other researchers, notably Peggy Li and Lila Gleitman, objected that the results might reflect the setting of the experiment and the wider culture rather than language itself, and they showed that English speakers could be led to adopt similar strategies when the test conditions were changed. The objection is fair, but it is not decisive. In real communities, language and culture develop together, and it may be impossible to separate their effects completely. Difficulty in establishing a cause is not evidence that there is no effect.
F

A 2001 study claimed that Mandarin speakers, whose language sometimes describes earlier and later events as 'up' and 'down', thought about time vertically in a way that English speakers did not. Several later attempts to reproduce the result failed. This does not prove that language has no influence on how people think about time; it shows only that one striking finding was less secure than it first appeared. It is, nevertheless, a warning against the appetite for surprising results that has made linguistic relativity such a popular subject for journalists.
G

The most defensible version of the idea, I would suggest, is captured by the psychologist Dan Slobin's phrase 'thinking for speaking'. Every language obliges its speakers to attend to certain details whenever they talk. A speaker of Turkish, for instance, is expected to indicate through grammar whether they witnessed a past event directly or learned of it from someone else. Over a lifetime of speaking, such requirements may become habits of attention, affecting what people notice and remember even when they are silent. On this account, language is less a prison than a well-worn path: one can always leave it, but it is the route most often taken.
H

This view has practical consequences for language learners. Learning a second language does not give anyone a capacity for thought they previously lacked, whatever some advertisements may promise. What it offers is something more modest but still valuable: practice in noticing distinctions that one's first language allows one to ignore. That is reason enough to take linguistic relativity seriously, without either inflating it into determinism or dismissing it as a myth.

title: Nature's Clean-up Crew
paras: A

Few animals have a less glamorous job than the dung beetle. Found on every continent except Antarctica, the more than 6,000 described species share a diet made up largely of the droppings of other animals. For a long time they attracted little attention outside specialist circles. Today, however, ecologists increasingly regard these insects as some of the most valuable workers in any grassland, forest or farm. By burying, eating and breaking up waste, they return nutrients to the soil, reduce the number of pests and may even help to limit the greenhouse gases released from animal waste on farms.
B

Scientists usually divide dung beetles into three groups according to how they deal with their food. 'Rollers' shape a portion of dung into a ball and push it away from the pile, sometimes for a considerable distance, before burying it. 'Tunnellers' dig straight down beneath a dung pat and drag material into chambers below the surface. 'Dwellers', the third group, simply live inside the pat itself, feeding and laying their eggs there without moving it at all. Rolling is the most famous behaviour, but in many habitats it is the tunnellers that move the largest quantities of dung into the ground.
C

The speed at which the beetles work can be remarkable. In East Africa, researchers once watched a fresh pile of elephant dung weighing about one and a half kilograms disappear within two hours as thousands of beetles arrived to claim a share. The insects locate their food by smell, and many species fly towards fresh droppings within minutes of them being produced. Competition is so intense that rollers must move their ball away quickly, because other beetles will try to steal it, and fights over a single ball are common.
D

Escaping from the crowd in a straight line is the safest strategy for a roller, and this requires a reliable sense of direction. Before setting off, a beetle often climbs on top of its ball and turns around slowly, a movement that researchers believe allows it to take a mental snapshot of the sky. Many species use the position of the sun, and at night the moon and the pattern of polarised light around it. In a well-known experiment, a South African species was found to keep its course on moonless nights by using the faint band of light from the Milky Way, making it the first animal known to navigate in this way. When researchers fitted the beetles with tiny caps that covered their eyes, the insects wandered in circles.
E

For farmers, the work of dung beetles has real economic value. When cattle dung is left on the surface of a field, it can remain there for weeks or even months, smothering the grass beneath and making the area unattractive to grazing animals, which avoid feeding close to droppings. It also provides breeding sites for flies and for the parasites of livestock. Beetles that bury dung quickly break this cycle. Their tunnels allow rainwater and air to reach deeper layers of soil, and the buried dung acts as a natural fertiliser for the grass. One study in the United States estimated that dung beetles save the country's cattle industry around 380 million dollars every year.
F

The importance of these insects became especially clear in Australia. When cattle were introduced there by European settlers, the native dung beetles, which had evolved to deal with the dry, pellet-like droppings of kangaroos and other marsupials, were unable to cope with the large, wet pats produced by cows. Dung piled up across pastures, and bush flies multiplied. In the 1960s scientists launched a national programme to import beetles from Africa and Europe, testing each species carefully to make sure it would not harm local wildlife. More than forty species were released, and about half of them became established. The project did not solve the problem everywhere, but it is often described as a successful example of biological control.
G

Despite their usefulness, dung beetle populations are declining in many regions. One cause is the widespread use of drugs to treat worms and other parasites in livestock. Some of these chemicals pass through the animal and remain active in its dung, where they can kill beetle larvae. The loss of natural grazing land and the disappearance of large wild mammals also reduce the beetles' food supply. Some ecologists now recommend that farmers treat their animals only when it is necessary and choose medicines that are less harmful to insects. As one researcher put it, protecting dung beetles costs very little, but losing them could prove extremely expensive.

title: Coffee and Commerce
paras: A

The first coffee house in England is usually said to have opened in Oxford in 1650, and two years later a similar establishment appeared in London, run by Pasqua Rosee, a servant who had acquired a taste for the drink while travelling in the eastern Mediterranean with his employer, a merchant. The bitter black liquid was at first regarded as an exotic curiosity, but it caught on with astonishing speed. Within a generation coffee houses could be found throughout the City of London, and by the early eighteenth century some observers claimed there were several hundred, although modern historians treat the higher estimates with caution.
B

Part of the attraction was price. In many houses a customer paid a penny at the door, and this bought not only a dish of coffee but the right to stay for as long as he wished, to read the newspapers lying on the tables and to join in the conversation. Because coffee, unlike ale or wine, did not intoxicate, discussion tended to remain reasonably orderly. Customers sat together at long tables, and convention held that anyone could take any available seat, so a shopkeeper might find himself beside a gentleman or a ship's captain. The houses were sometimes nicknamed 'penny universities' because of the education in news and argument that could be had for the price of a drink.
C

For merchants, the most valuable thing a coffee house offered was information. In an age long before the telegraph, it was difficult to know when a ship had arrived, what goods were selling for in Amsterdam or whether a trading partner was still able to pay his debts. Coffee house owners competed for customers by subscribing to newspapers, collecting letters and posting notices of ship movements and auctions. As a result, customers with similar interests began to gather in particular houses, and over time individual coffee houses became associated with particular trades, from shipping and insurance to books and the law.
D

The best-known example is the house opened by Edward Lloyd in about 1688. Lloyd's attracted sea captains, ship owners and merchants, and Lloyd took care to supply them with reliable shipping news, eventually publishing it in a sheet of his own. It was here that the business of marine insurance took shape. A merchant wishing to protect a voyage would have the details of the ship and its cargo written on a sheet of paper, and individuals willing to accept a share of the risk would write their names underneath, together with the amount they would cover. This practice gave rise to the term 'underwriter', still used in insurance today. In the 1770s the underwriters formed their own society and moved to premises elsewhere, but the name of the coffee house survives in Lloyd's of London.
E

A similar story can be told about the trading of shares. Dealers in company stock had a poor reputation for noisy and aggressive behaviour, and they were not welcome at the Royal Exchange, the grand building where respectable merchants met. Many of them instead conducted their business in the coffee houses of Exchange Alley nearby, especially one called Jonathan's. From 1698 a broker named John Castaing issued a regular list of the prices of shares and goods from Jonathan's, one of the earliest publications of its kind. In 1773 a group of brokers put up their own building close by and, after some debate, called it the Stock Exchange.
F

Not everyone approved of these new institutions. Critics complained that men wasted whole days in idle talk, and in 1674 a pamphlet presented as a complaint by the women of London protested that the drink was keeping husbands away from home. The government had more serious concerns. Coffee houses were places where political news, rumour and criticism circulated freely, and in December 1675 King Charles II issued a proclamation ordering them to close. The reaction was so hostile, not least from the many traders who depended on them, that the order was withdrawn within a matter of days, before it had even come into effect.
G

The decline of the coffee house, when it came in the later eighteenth century, was gradual. The institutions that had grown up inside them needed private premises, formal membership and rules, while exclusive gentlemen's clubs offered a more comfortable setting for the wealthy. At the same time tea, heavily promoted by the East India Company, was replacing coffee as the national drink. Historians continue to debate how much the coffee houses really mattered. Dr Miriam Hale describes them as 'nothing less than the first offices of modern finance'. Professor Tomas Reyes is more cautious, arguing that insurance and share dealing would have found a home somewhere and that coffee houses were simply the most convenient rooms available. For Dr Alan Fielding, the lasting change was cultural: the coffee house taught merchants to trust written, published information exchanged among people who did not know one another personally.

title: The Case for Difficulty
paras: A

Almost every new piece of educational technology arrives with the same promise: it will make learning easier. Apps offer to explain a difficult equation in seconds, translation tools remove the labour of looking up words, and the latest generation of AI assistants will summarise a chapter, draft an essay outline or check a proof at any hour of the day. The promise is attractive, and it is usually sincere. The people who build these tools are not, for the most part, trying to deceive anyone; they genuinely believe that removing obstacles from a learner's path is a kindness. My argument is that this belief, however well meant, rests on a misunderstanding of how learning actually works.
B

In commercial software, 'friction' is a dirty word. Every extra click, every moment of confusion, is something to be designed away, because friction causes customers to abandon a purchase. It is understandable that the same philosophy has been carried into products for students. But a learner is not a customer trying to complete a transaction as quickly as possible. The point of solving a problem in mathematics is not to obtain the answer, which is usually printed at the back of the book, but to change something in the mind of the person solving it. If the tool does the work, the transaction is completed and the change never happens.
C

Cognitive psychology has a name for the kinds of effort that help rather than hinder. Robert and Elizabeth Bjork, psychologists at the University of California, Los Angeles, call them 'desirable difficulties'. Their research, and a large body of work that has followed it, suggests that conditions which make learning feel slower and harder in the moment often produce far better long-term retention. These include testing yourself instead of re-reading, spacing practice out over several days rather than cramming it into one evening, and mixing different types of problem together. The act of struggling to recall a half-remembered fact appears to strengthen the memory itself. Remove the struggle, and you weaken the result.
D

What makes this finding awkward is that learners themselves are poor judges of it. When students re-read a textbook chapter, the material feels increasingly familiar, and familiarity is easily mistaken for understanding. Psychologists call this the illusion of fluency. Surveys of university students repeatedly find that re-reading and highlighting are among the most common revision strategies, while self-testing, which is considerably more effective, is used far less. A tool that produces a neat summary on demand risks intensifying this illusion: the summary is clear, the student nods along, and the knowledge that seemed so secure has gone a week later.
E

An analogy may help. Imagine a gym that installed machines to lift the weights for its members. Attendance would probably rise, sessions would feel pleasant, and members would report high levels of satisfaction. Nobody, however, would become any stronger. The effort is not an unfortunate side effect of the exercise; it is the exercise. Much of what we call learning is similar, and a technology that removes the effort may remove the benefit along with it.
F

The problem is made worse by the way educational products are often evaluated. Because long-term learning is slow and expensive to measure, companies, and sometimes schools, rely on figures that are easy to collect: how many minutes students spend in an app, how many lessons they complete, how highly they rate the experience. These engagement metrics are not worthless, but they reward exactly the qualities that desirable difficulties lack. A product that makes students feel confident and entertained will score well, whether or not they can remember anything a month later. In effect, we have built a measurement system that cannot see the thing we care about most.
G

None of this is an argument for removing technology from classrooms, a response that some head teachers and politicians have recently favoured. Banning devices is a blunt instrument. It throws away the genuine advantages of digital tools, such as instant feedback on practice questions, access to far more material than a school library could ever hold, and the ability to adapt the pace of work to individual students. It also does little to prepare young people for a world in which such tools will be everywhere. The more useful question is not whether learners should use technology, but what kind of effort it asks of them.
H

Some designers are already taking this question seriously. There are tutoring programs that respond to a wrong answer not by revealing the correct one but by offering a hint and asking the student to try again, and flashcard applications built around spaced retrieval rather than repeated viewing. An AI assistant could equally be configured to ask questions rather than answer them, or to withhold a summary until the student has attempted one of their own. Such tools will rarely top a ranking of user satisfaction, and that is precisely why teachers, rather than app stores, should decide which ones are used. Good teaching has always involved knowing when to help and when to step back. Our tools should be built to know the same thing.

title: Ice in the Desert
paras: A

For most of human history, keeping food cool in a hot climate was a serious challenge. Yet in the dry interior of what is now Iran, people were storing ice through the summer more than two thousand years ago, long before electricity or mechanical refrigeration. They did so using a remarkable building known as the yakhchāl, a Persian word that literally means 'ice pit'. Several hundred of these structures are thought to have existed at one time, and dozens survive today, some of them restored as tourist attractions.
B

At first sight, a yakhchāl looks like a giant beehive rising out of the desert. The visible part is a tall dome, often around 18 metres high, built from mud brick. But the dome is only half of the story. Beneath it lies a deep pit, sometimes holding several thousand cubic metres of space, where the ice was actually kept. Because the pit was underground, it was protected from the fierce daytime heat, while the ground around it stayed at a fairly constant temperature throughout the year.
C

The ice itself was not brought from distant mountains, as many visitors assume. Instead, it was made on site during the winter. Desert regions such as central Iran can be extremely hot by day but surprisingly cold at night, particularly between December and February, when temperatures regularly fall below freezing. Builders took advantage of this by constructing long, shallow channels or pools next to the yakhchāl. On cold evenings, water was released into these pools, often from a qanat, an underground canal that carried water from distant hills. Being only a few centimetres deep, the water froze quickly overnight. The following morning, workers broke the ice into blocks and carried them down into the pit.
D

To make freezing more reliable, a high wall was usually built along the southern side of the pools. This wall, which could be more than ten metres tall, kept the sun off the water during the short winter days, so that ice formed during one night was not melted the next afternoon. It also helped to block warm winds. In some places the process was repeated night after night for weeks, with each new layer of ice added to the store until the pit was full.
E

Keeping the ice frozen for the rest of the year depended largely on the materials used. The walls at the base of the dome could be two metres thick, and they were covered with a special mortar called sārooj. Accounts of its exact recipe vary, but it is generally said to have contained sand, clay, lime, ash and goat hair, and in some versions egg whites. This mixture was highly resistant to water and did not allow heat to pass through easily. The ice blocks were also separated by layers of straw or chaff, which acted as insulation and made it easier to remove one block without disturbing the rest.
F

The shape of the dome was equally important. Warm air rises, so any heat that entered the building collected at the top of the dome, well above the stored ice. A small opening at the summit allowed some of this warm air to escape, while cooler air sank towards the pit. Some yakhchāls were also connected to windcatchers, tower-like structures that directed breezes downwards into a building. Any water from melting ice ran into a trench at the bottom of the pit, where it could refreeze during cold nights or be drained away.
G

Ice from the yakhchāl had many uses. It was used to keep meat and dairy products fresh, and it allowed the preparation of cold desserts such as fālūdeh, a dish of thin noodles in a frozen syrup that is still popular in Iran today. In the hottest months, wealthy households bought ice to cool drinks, and some historians believe that ordinary townspeople could also purchase small quantities at a modest price. In many towns the yakhchāl was a shared public facility rather than private property, and its upkeep was an important civic responsibility.
H

The arrival of electric refrigerators in the twentieth century made these buildings unnecessary, and many were abandoned or demolished. Recently, however, architects and engineers have shown renewed interest in them. With rising energy costs and concern about climate change, they see the yakhchāl as a valuable example of passive cooling, the use of design rather than machines to control temperature. While nobody suggests returning to ice pits, the principles behind them, such as thick insulating walls, careful shading and the natural movement of air, are being studied for use in modern buildings in hot, dry regions.

title: Cities in the Shade
paras: A

As summers grow hotter, city governments around the world are rethinking an element of urban design that was long taken for granted: shade. For much of the twentieth century, planners in many countries concentrated on moving cars efficiently and providing sunlight to buildings, particularly in cooler northern climates where daylight was scarce in winter. Shade, if it was considered at all, was treated as a by-product of trees planted for decoration. Today, a growing number of researchers argue that shade should be regarded as essential public infrastructure, as important to the health of a city as drainage or street lighting.
B

The case rests partly on the difference between air temperature and what people actually feel. Weather reports describe the temperature of the air in the shade, but a person walking along an exposed pavement at midday also absorbs direct radiation from the sun and heat given off by surrounding surfaces. Climate scientist Dr Helena Varga, who has measured conditions on city streets for over a decade, points out that the 'felt' temperature on a sunny pavement can be 15 to 20 degrees higher than in a shaded spot only a few metres away, even when the air temperature in both places is identical. 'Two people on the same street can be experiencing completely different climates,' she says.
C

Traditional architecture in hot regions reflects this understanding. In the old quarters of many Mediterranean and Middle Eastern towns, streets are narrow and often winding, so that buildings shade one another for most of the day. Covered walkways, arcades and courtyards provide further protection, and in some markets fabric is stretched between rooftops to shelter shoppers. Architectural historian Samuel Okoro believes these features were not simply accidents of crowded medieval life. 'Builders who had no air conditioning were forced to observe the sun's path very carefully,' he argues. 'Their solutions were the result of centuries of trial and error.'
D

Modern cities, by contrast, have often been designed in ways that remove shade. Wide roads, large car parks and open plazas paved in concrete or stone leave pedestrians exposed, while dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. This contributes to the so-called urban heat island effect, in which a city remains noticeably warmer than the surrounding countryside after sunset. Glass towers can add to the problem by reflecting sunlight down onto the street below. The result, according to urban planner Mia Lindqvist, is that many recently built districts are uncomfortable to walk through for several hours a day in summer, which encourages people to drive even for short journeys.
E

Trees are the most familiar solution, and they offer more than shade alone. Through a process called transpiration, they release water vapour from their leaves, which cools the air around them. A single mature tree can therefore have a cooling effect comparable to several air-conditioning units. However, trees take decades to reach full size, and they need space for their roots, regular watering and protection from damage, all of which can be difficult to provide beneath crowded pavements full of pipes and cables. Lindqvist notes that young trees planted in small holes surrounded by concrete frequently die within a few years, wasting the money spent on them.
F

For this reason, some cities are combining trees with built forms of shade. These range from simple canopies over bus stops and playgrounds to large structures such as the shade sails that cover public squares in some Spanish and Australian cities. Engineers are also experimenting with materials that reflect rather than absorb sunlight, including pale-coloured pavements and 'cool roofs'. Varga cautions, though, that reflective surfaces must be placed carefully: a bright pavement can bounce heat back up onto pedestrians, making them feel hotter rather than cooler, even if it lowers the surface temperature itself.
G

Perhaps the greatest obstacle is not technical but organisational. In most cities, responsibility for streets, parks, buildings and public health is divided between separate departments, each with its own budget and priorities, and no single body is in charge of shade. A few cities have begun to address this by drawing up shade plans, which map where shelter is lacking and set targets for increasing it, often giving priority to routes used by children, older people and those waiting for public transport. Okoro sees this as a return to an older way of thinking. 'For most of history,' he says, 'designing for shade was simply part of designing a city. We are now rediscovering what our ancestors knew.'

title: Measuring the Wrong Thing?
paras: A

When a new medicine is tested, the question that matters most to patients is simple: will it help me live longer, or live better? Answering that question directly, however, can take many years and require tens of thousands of participants, because the events that researchers ultimately care about, such as heart attacks, strokes or deaths, may occur in only a small fraction of those enrolled. Understandably, then, medical science has come to rely heavily on shortcuts. Rather than waiting for these 'hard' outcomes, trials often measure a so-called surrogate endpoint: a laboratory value or physical sign, such as blood pressure, cholesterol level or the size of a tumour on a scan, that is expected to predict the outcome of real interest.
B

The appeal of surrogates is obvious, and I do not wish to suggest that they have no place in research. A change in blood sugar can be detected within weeks; a reduction in deaths from diabetes might take a decade to appear. By allowing treatments to be evaluated quickly and cheaply, surrogates have undoubtedly brought some valuable drugs to patients sooner than would otherwise have been possible. For people with rare or rapidly fatal diseases, for whom a long trial is simply not an option, this speed can make an enormous difference. My concern is not that surrogates are used, but that they are too often trusted beyond what the evidence can bear.
C

The fundamental problem is that a measurement may be associated with a disease without lying on the path that causes harm. Consider an analogy. Grey hair is strongly associated with age, and age with mortality, yet no one would expect hair dye to extend life. Few surrogates are as obviously misleading as this, but the logic is the same: a drug may improve the number that doctors are watching while leaving the underlying disease untouched, or it may act on the disease through one mechanism while causing damage through another that the surrogate fails to detect.
D

History provides sobering examples. In the 1980s, doctors knew that patients who experienced certain irregular heartbeats after a heart attack were more likely to die suddenly. It seemed reasonable to assume that drugs which suppressed these irregular rhythms would save lives, and such drugs were widely prescribed on precisely that basis. When a large trial finally tested the assumption, however, it found that patients receiving some of the drugs were dying at a substantially higher rate than those given a placebo. The surrogate had moved in the desired direction; the patients had not. Similar stories, though usually less dramatic, can be told about treatments that improved cholesterol readings or bone density without delivering the expected benefit.
E

Defenders of current practice reply that such cases are exceptions, and that regulators now demand stronger evidence before approving drugs on the basis of surrogates alone. There is some truth in this. Many agencies grant early approval only on condition that manufacturers carry out confirmatory trials measuring hard outcomes after the drug reaches the market. Yet studies of these arrangements have repeatedly found that confirmatory trials are delayed for years, are designed in ways that make clear answers unlikely, or are never completed at all. Meanwhile, the drug is prescribed to many thousands of people, and once a treatment has become established, there is little commercial incentive to discover that it does not work.
F

A subtler difficulty is that a surrogate validated for one treatment may not be valid for another. Even if lowering blood pressure with one class of drug reduces strokes, a new drug that lowers blood pressure by a different biological route might not do the same, because its other effects on the body are unknown. Researchers sometimes speak as though a surrogate, once accepted, is permanently reliable. In my view, this is a category error: what has been validated is the relationship between a particular intervention, a particular measurement and a particular outcome, not the measurement in general.
G

None of this means that we should abandon surrogates, which would bring the development of many treatments almost to a halt. What it does mean is that their limitations should be stated far more honestly, both by researchers and by those who report on their work. Press releases announcing that a drug 'shrinks tumours' or 'cuts cholesterol' frequently imply that it saves lives, which may or may not be true. Patients deciding whether to accept a treatment deserve to know whether its benefits have been shown on outcomes they care about, or merely on numbers in a laboratory report.
H

There are also practical steps that could reduce the risk. Regulators could set firm deadlines for confirmatory trials and withdraw approval when these are missed. Trials could be designed to collect information on hard outcomes from the beginning, even if the initial decision is based on a surrogate. And large databases of patient records, now increasingly available, could be used to monitor whether the benefits suggested by early studies actually appear in everyday practice. Surrogates are, at best, informed guesses about the future. The danger lies not in making such guesses, but in forgetting that that is all they are.

title: Sealed for the Journey: A Short History of the Tin Can
paras: A

In 1795, France was at war on several fronts, and its armies were suffering more from hunger and scurvy than from enemy fire. The government offered a prize of 12,000 francs to anyone who could devise a reliable method of keeping food edible for long periods. The challenge was taken up by Nicolas Appert, a Parisian confectioner and brewer who had spent years experimenting in his kitchen. Appert had no scientific explanation for why food spoiled; the work of Louis Pasteur on micro-organisms lay more than half a century in the future. What he had was patience and a practical observation: food that was sealed in an airtight container and then heated thoroughly would stay fresh for months.
B

Appert's method used thick glass bottles, which he filled with soups, vegetables, fruit and even whole partridges. He closed the necks with cork, wired the corks in place, and then plunged the bottles into boiling water for periods that varied according to the contents. In 1806 samples were sent to sea with the French navy, and after several months the meat and vegetables were found to be in excellent condition. Appert was awarded the prize in 1810 on the condition that he publish his technique, which he did in a book with the lengthy title The Art of Preserving All Kinds of Animal and Vegetable Substances for Several Years. He used the money to open what is often described as the world's first commercial canning factory, although it produced bottles rather than cans.
C

Glass, however, had obvious disadvantages for armies and navies. It was heavy, and it broke easily when carts jolted along rough roads or ships rolled in heavy seas. Within months of Appert's publication, an English merchant named Peter Durand obtained a patent for preserving food in containers made of tin-plated iron. Durand does not seem to have manufactured anything himself; he sold the patent for £1,000 to Bryan Donkin and John Hall, who set up a factory in south London in 1812. By 1813 they were supplying canned beef, mutton and vegetable soup to the Royal Navy, and the Duke of Wellington is reported to have tasted their products and found them acceptable.
D

Early cans were far from convenient. Each one was made by hand: a skilled tinsmith cut the metal, shaped it around a mould and soldered the seams, and a good worker might produce only sixty cans in a day. The cans were also extremely solid, with walls often thicker than those of modern containers, and they carried no means of opening them. Instructions on some early naval rations advised the user to cut around the top with a chisel and hammer. Soldiers in the field were known to use bayonets, knives or even rifle fire. The first dedicated can opener did not appear until 1858, almost half a century after the can itself, and the familiar rotating-wheel design was not patented until 1870.
E

Safety was a second problem. Because nobody understood the science behind the process, manufacturers had no reliable way to decide how long a can needed to be heated. Some producers shortened heating times to increase output, and the results could be disastrous. In 1845 a British expedition led by Sir John Franklin set out to find a sea route through the Arctic, carrying thousands of cans of food. None of the 129 men returned. Later investigators suggested that poorly soldered cans may have exposed the crew to lead, although historians continue to debate how much this contributed to the tragedy compared with cold, scurvy and starvation.
F

Change came in the second half of the nineteenth century from two directions. First, Pasteur's research in the 1860s showed that spoilage was caused by living organisms, which gave canners a scientific basis for their work. Second, the introduction of pressure cookers into factories allowed cans to be heated to temperatures above the boiling point of water, which killed bacteria far more efficiently and reduced processing time. At the same time, machines began to replace hand labour. By the 1880s, automated lines in the United States could produce thousands of cans an hour, and the price of canned food fell sharply.
G

Demand grew as prices fell. The American Civil War in the 1860s had already introduced large numbers of soldiers to canned meat and vegetables, and many continued to buy them after returning home. In cities, where fresh produce was often expensive out of season, canned tomatoes, peaches and condensed milk became ordinary household items. Brand names began to appear on brightly printed labels, and companies competed to persuade shoppers that their products were clean, modern and trustworthy. The can had moved from the battlefield to the kitchen cupboard.
H

Today the basic principle remains the one Appert discovered: seal the food, then heat it. Modern cans are made of thinner steel or aluminium, the seams are sealed by machine rather than soldered, and the inside surface is usually coated to stop the metal reacting with acidic foods. Yet the story of the can is a reminder that a technology can be adopted widely long before anyone fully understands why it works. For more than fifty years, millions of people trusted a method whose success was, in scientific terms, a mystery.

title: Meadows Beneath the Waves
paras: A

Ask most people to name the ecosystems that help to slow climate change, and they will mention rainforests. Few will think of the shallow, sunlit waters along the world's coasts, where flowering plants called seagrasses form dense underwater meadows. Seagrasses are not seaweeds, which are algae; they are true plants, descended from land-dwelling ancestors that returned to the sea roughly 100 million years ago. They have roots, leaves and flowers, and some species even release pollen into the water. Although they cover less than 0.2 per cent of the ocean floor, a growing body of research suggests that they store a remarkably large share of the carbon buried in marine sediments each year, with some estimates putting the figure at around ten per cent.
B

The secret lies less in the plants themselves than in what happens beneath them. Like any plant, a seagrass absorbs carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and uses it to build leaves and roots. But a meadow also acts as a trap. Its leaves slow the movement of water, so that tiny particles of organic matter drifting in the current, including fragments of dead plankton and material washed from the land, settle on the seabed rather than being carried away. These particles are then buried by sediment. Because the mud below a meadow contains very little oxygen, the microbes that would normally break down this material work extremely slowly. As a result, carbon can remain locked in the sediment not for decades, as in many forests, but for thousands of years. Dr Helena Varga, a marine ecologist who has taken sediment cores in the Mediterranean, found carbon-rich layers beneath one meadow that were more than 4,000 years old.
C

This long-term storage has led scientists to coin the term 'blue carbon' for carbon captured by coastal ecosystems, including mangrove forests and salt marshes as well as seagrass. Interest in blue carbon has grown rapidly over the past fifteen years, partly because governments and companies are searching for ways to offset emissions they cannot easily reduce. If the carbon stored in a restored meadow could be measured reliably, it might be sold as credits, providing money for conservation. Several pilot schemes are already under way, although none has yet operated long enough to prove its value.
D

The difficulty is that seagrass meadows are disappearing. Studies of records from around the world indicate that about a third of the global area has been lost since the late nineteenth century, and in some regions the rate of loss accelerated in the late twentieth century. The causes are mostly local. Nutrients from farm fertiliser and sewage encourage the growth of algae, which cloud the water and block the light the seagrass needs. Dredging for ports, boat anchors and coastal construction tear up the plants directly. Rising sea temperatures add further stress: during a marine heatwave off Western Australia in 2011, large areas of meadow in Shark Bay died within weeks. When a meadow is destroyed, the sediment it held in place can be washed away, and the carbon it contains may be released back into the water and eventually the atmosphere.
E

Restoration, therefore, seems an obvious response, but it has a mixed history. Early attempts in the 1980s and 1990s often involved transplanting adult plants from healthy meadows, an expensive process that damaged the donor sites and frequently failed. A more successful approach was developed in Virginia, on the east coast of the United States, where seagrass had vanished from coastal bays after a disease outbreak in the 1930s. Beginning in 1999, researchers and volunteers collected millions of seeds and scattered them by hand from small boats. Professor Daniel Okafor, who has studied the project for over a decade, describes the result as 'better than anyone predicted'. The restored meadows now cover more than 3,600 hectares, and measurements show that the sediment beneath them is steadily accumulating carbon. Okafor stresses, however, that success depended on a condition that cannot be created artificially in the short term: the water quality in the bays was already good.
F

Not all scientists share the enthusiasm for seagrass as a climate solution. Dr Mei Lin Tan, a biogeochemist, points out that some of the carbon found under meadows originally came from elsewhere, such as rivers or nearby forests, and might have been buried anyway. Counting it as a benefit of the meadow could exaggerate the climate value of restoration. She also notes that seagrass sediments can produce small amounts of methane, and that animals living in the meadows release carbon dioxide as they build their shells. In her view, these factors do not cancel out the benefits, but they mean that carbon accounts must be calculated with great care. Varga accepts that the measurements are complex, but argues that uncertainty should not become an excuse for doing nothing.
G

Even the most optimistic researchers accept that seagrass cannot compensate for continued fossil fuel use. The total amount of carbon these meadows could absorb, even if all lost areas were restored, is small compared with global emissions. Their wider value may lie elsewhere. Meadows shelter young fish, including commercially important species, filter coastal water, and reduce the force of waves reaching the shore. Protecting them, many ecologists argue, makes sense whatever their precise role in the carbon budget.

title: Should Beauty Guide Physics?
paras: A

Physicists are not usually thought of as connoisseurs of beauty, yet the language of aesthetics runs through the history of their discipline. Paul Dirac, whose equation describing the electron predicted the existence of antimatter, declared that it was more important for a theory to be beautiful than to agree with experiment. Einstein is said to have been so confident in general relativity that, asked what he would have done had observations contradicted it, he replied that he would have felt sorry for God. Such remarks are often repeated with admiration. I want to suggest that they deserve rather more suspicion than they usually receive.
B

It would be foolish to deny that aesthetic judgement has played a productive role in science. When two theories explain the same data, scientists routinely prefer the one that makes fewer assumptions, and there are good reasons for doing so. A theory with fewer adjustable parts is harder to rescue when it fails, and therefore says more about the world. In this limited sense, simplicity is not a matter of taste at all but a practical virtue. Elegance can also serve as a useful signal during research: a calculation that suddenly becomes neat may indicate that the investigator has found the right variables. Many working scientists report precisely this experience, and I see no reason to doubt them.
C

The trouble begins when beauty is treated not as a guide to where truth might be found, but as a substitute for evidence. The historical record is less flattering to the aesthetic approach than its defenders admit. Johannes Kepler spent years trying to show that the orbits of the planets were determined by the five perfect solids of geometry, a scheme he regarded as divinely beautiful. It was wrong. His lasting achievement, the discovery that planetary orbits are ellipses, came only when he abandoned the circles that astronomers since antiquity had considered the most perfect of shapes. In this case, progress required giving up beauty rather than pursuing it. Nineteenth-century physicists, too, found the idea that atoms were tiny whirlpools in an invisible fluid extraordinarily elegant; the theory occupied serious minds for decades and left almost nothing behind.
D

The success stories, meanwhile, are vulnerable to a familiar bias. We remember Dirac's equation because it was confirmed; the many attractive theories that were not have largely been forgotten, along with the confidence of their authors. If beauty were genuinely reliable, we would expect the proportion of beautiful theories that turn out to be true to be noticeably higher than the proportion of ugly ones. Nobody has shown this, and it is not obvious how it could be shown, since judgements of beauty are often made after a theory has already been accepted. Familiarity breeds affection: quantum mechanics struck many of its founders as ugly and arbitrary, and it is only after a century of success that textbooks describe it as profound and elegant.
E

Why should any of this matter now? Because in some areas of fundamental physics the gap between theory and experiment has become very wide. Certain proposals concern energies far beyond the reach of any conceivable particle accelerator, and their supporters have sometimes defended them on the grounds that they are too elegant to be false. Critics within the field have warned that this amounts to a quiet change in the rules of science, in which mathematical attractiveness takes the place of observation. If that change is allowed to continue, decisions about which research to fund and which young scientists to hire may come to depend on a shared aesthetic rather than on results, and a whole generation could be trained to admire the same untested ideas.
F

One response is to argue that aesthetic preferences in physics are not arbitrary but have been shaped by centuries of contact with nature, so that physicists' sense of beauty has, in effect, been trained by the universe itself. There is something to this. Yet a sense trained on past successes is, by definition, a sense trained on the kinds of theory that worked before. It may be poorly suited to recognising the kind of theory that will work next, especially if, as has happened repeatedly, nature turns out to be stranger than anyone expected. Kepler's ellipses and the probabilities of quantum mechanics both offended the aesthetic expectations of their day.
G

None of this means that scientists should stop talking about beauty, or that the pleasure they take in an elegant result is somehow illegitimate. Aesthetic response is part of what draws people into science and keeps them there through years of frustrating work. Nor am I proposing that elegance should be ignored when choosing which ideas to explore first; with limited time and money, researchers must start somewhere, and an attractive idea is as reasonable a starting point as any. My claim is narrower: that beauty may properly influence where scientists look, but never what they conclude. A theory earns belief by surviving tests it could have failed, not by moving those who study it.
H

Perhaps the most telling evidence comes from scientists themselves. Asked privately, many will admit that the theories they found most beautiful as students were not the ones that proved most important in their careers. That is a modest observation, but it points in the right direction. Beauty, like intuition, is a valuable servant and a poor master.

title: Measuring Without a Yardstick: Thermometry and the Problem of Circularity
paras: A

Few instruments seem as innocent as the thermometer. We glance at it, read off a number and assume that the number reports a fact about the world. Yet the history of thermometry raises a question that is far from innocent. To know that a thermometer measures temperature accurately, one would need to compare its readings with the true temperature; but the only way of finding out the true temperature is to use a thermometer. Philosophers of science have come to regard this as a paradigm case of what is sometimes called the problem of nomic measurement: the difficulty of establishing a measuring procedure when the law connecting the observable reading to the quantity of interest can itself be tested only by measuring that quantity.
B

The earliest instruments sidestepped the difficulty rather than solving it. The thermoscopes of the early seventeenth century, typically a glass bulb attached to a tube whose open end stood in a vessel of water, registered changes in warmth as the water rose or fell in the tube. They could show that one room was warmer than another, but they carried no scale, and so offered an ordering of hot and cold rather than a quantity. Nor were their readings stable: because the tube was open, the water level responded to fluctuations in atmospheric pressure as well as to heat, so that a change in the weather could masquerade as a change in temperature. Sealing the instrument removed this particular confusion, but it did nothing to settle what the numbers on a scale, once added, actually meant.
C

The obvious strategy was to anchor the scale to phenomena that occur at a fixed temperature, and the freezing and boiling of water were the natural candidates. The strategy, however, quietly presupposes what it sets out to establish, since the assumption that these phenomena are constant could only be checked with a reliable thermometer. Nor did nature cooperate. Eighteenth-century investigators found that water would sometimes rise well above its customary boiling point before erupting violently, and that the degree of this superheating seemed to depend on how much air the water contained and on the material and cleanliness of the vessel. The eventual solution was to take as the fixed point not the boiling water itself but the steam above it, whose temperature proved far less sensitive to such circumstances. The choice was less a discovery than a decision, albeit one informed by careful observation of which phenomenon behaved most stably.
D

Fixed points, moreover, solve only half the problem. Once two points have been marked and the interval divided into equal degrees, one has implicitly assumed that the thermometric fluid expands uniformly as it is heated, so that equal increases in volume correspond to equal increases in temperature. Instruments filled with mercury and with alcohol could be made to agree at both fixed points, yet between them they diverged, sometimes by several degrees. At least one of the two fluids, then, must expand irregularly; but to determine which, one would have to compare each against the true temperature, and the circle closes once again.
E

The most influential way out of this impasse was, paradoxically, to stop asking which instrument was correct. Nineteenth-century experimenters began to judge a type of thermometer by whether instruments of that type, constructed by different makers from different batches of material, agreed with one another. By this test of comparability, mercury thermometers performed disappointingly, because the glass that held the mercury varied in its own expansion from one batch to the next. Thermometers that used air as their working substance, by contrast, gave strikingly consistent results. It is worth stressing what this criterion did not show. Agreement among air thermometers demonstrated that they were reproducible, not that they tracked temperature itself; a whole family of instruments could, in principle, share a common error. Comparability was a pragmatic standard, adopted precisely because a more ambitious one was unavailable.
F

A theoretical escape seemed to appear in the middle of the nineteenth century, when an absolute scale of temperature was defined in terms of the efficiency of an idealised heat engine, with no reference to the properties of any particular substance. No such engine can be built, however, so in practice the absolute scale had to be realised by means of gas thermometers, corrected for the ways in which real gases depart from ideal behaviour, and those corrections were calculated from theory that had itself been tested with thermometers. Some philosophers have nonetheless argued that the circle is better described as a spiral. On this account, sometimes labelled epistemic iteration, each stage begins from standards that are accepted provisionally and then uses them to detect and correct their own shortcomings, so that later standards improve on the earlier ones that made them possible.
G

The iterative picture has not gone unchallenged. Critics point out that a sequence of mutual corrections might converge, with great precision, on an error that is self-consistent but nonetheless an error: coherence among our instruments, they insist, is not the same thing as correspondence to the world. Defenders reply that the spiral is not sealed off from that world. Successive standards are constrained by a variety of physical phenomena that have no obvious reason to conspire, and when methods built on quite different principles, such as the expansion of a gas and the speed of sound in it, converge on the same values, an undetected shared error becomes increasingly hard to believe in.
H

The questions are not merely historical. In 2019 the kelvin was redefined by fixing the numerical value of a constant of nature, so that the unit no longer rests on a property of water. The change is sometimes presented as the moment at which temperature finally acquired a secure foundation. A reader of the history might draw a more modest conclusion: that the foundations of measurement are not discovered beneath our practices but built up within them, through a long negotiation between theory, instrument and judgement.

title: Does Language Shape Thought? The Long Afterlife of Linguistic Relativity
paras: A

Few ideas in the study of language have been declared dead as often, or revived as persistently, as the claim that the language we speak shapes the way we think. In its popular form, usually attributed to the American linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf, the hypothesis holds that speakers of different languages inhabit, in some measure, different mental worlds. For much of the twentieth century the idea enjoyed a reputation out of all proportion to the evidence offered for it; for several decades after that, it was treated by many cognitive scientists as an embarrassment, a romantic notion that serious researchers had outgrown. Its current status is harder to summarise, partly because the question itself has been quietly reformulated.
B

Whorf's own arguments rested largely on comparisons between the grammar of English and that of Hopi, a language of the American Southwest, which he claimed lacked words and grammatical forms referring to time as a quantity that could be counted or divided. From this he inferred that Hopi speakers conceived of time quite differently from Europeans. Later fieldwork cast serious doubt on the linguistic premise, documenting a range of temporal expressions in Hopi that Whorf had overlooked or misdescribed. Yet even had his description been accurate, the inference would have been fragile, for it moved directly from differences in language to differences in thought without any independent measure of the latter. The circularity is easy to miss: if the only evidence that two groups think differently is that they speak differently, the claim that language shapes thought has not been tested at all.
C

It was this methodological weakness, rather than any single refutation, that pushed the hypothesis to the margins. From the 1960s onwards, influential research on colour suggested that the way languages divide up the spectrum is far from arbitrary: languages with only a few basic colour words appeared to select them from a predictable set, and speakers of such languages seemed to pick out the same best examples of a colour as speakers of languages with many more terms. To many, these findings implied that perception was anchored in human physiology rather than in vocabulary. At the same time, the rise of theories that treated the capacity for language as a largely universal endowment encouraged the view that beneath surface differences, all human minds operate in fundamentally similar ways.
D

The revival, when it came, owed less to new theory than to new methods. Instead of inferring thought from language, researchers began to devise non-linguistic tasks, such as sorting objects, remembering arrangements or judging whether two colour patches were identical, and to compare the performance of speakers of different languages on them. Ingrid Halvorsen, whose work on spatial reasoning helped to define this approach, has argued that the crucial step was to stop asking whether language determines thought and to ask instead where, when and how much it makes a difference. Her studies of communities whose languages describe location in terms of fixed directions, roughly equivalent to north and south, rather than left and right, found that their members tended to reconstruct a scene according to compass bearings even when no words were required.
E

Not everyone is persuaded that such results reveal anything deep. Tomás Arredondo, a psycholinguist who has spent much of his career replicating relativity experiments, accepts that many of the effects are genuine but argues that they are frequently produced by the participants quietly putting the task into words to themselves. When this inner speech is blocked, for example by asking participants to repeat a string of digits while they perform the task, several well-known effects shrink markedly or disappear. For Arredondo, this suggests that language functions less as a lens that permanently alters perception than as a tool that people pick up when it helps. Others have pointed out that groups compared in such studies typically differ in culture, environment and schooling as well as in language, so that attributing their differences to language alone may be premature.
F

Supporters of a moderate relativity have responded by narrowing their claims rather than abandoning them. Priya Ramanathan, who studies colour discrimination, observes that the fact that an effect depends on language being active at the moment of the task does not make it trivial, since in everyday life language is seldom switched off. She has also stressed that her findings concern speed and ease, not possibility: speakers whose language divides a region of the spectrum into two named categories tell shades across that boundary apart slightly faster than those whose language does not, yet both groups are perfectly capable of seeing the difference. Kenji Morimoto, meanwhile, has argued that the most durable effects may lie not in perception at all but in what people habitually attend to and remember, such as whether an event was intentional, when grammar obliges speakers to mark it.
G

What emerges from these exchanges is a hypothesis that has been reduced in scope while gaining in credibility. Hardly anyone now defends the claim that a language confines its speakers to thoughts it can express, and few would deny that languages can nudge attention and memory in particular directions. The disagreement lies in the territory between these positions: whether the effects are lasting or momentary, central to cognition or peripheral, and whether they stem from language as such or from the cultural practices it accompanies. It would be too strong to say the debate has been settled; it would be fairer to say it has at last been posed in a form that evidence can address.
