title: Binding the Future Self: The Promise and Limits of Commitment Devices
paras: A

In the most famous scene of the Odyssey, Ulysses orders his crew to tie him to the mast so that he can hear the song of the Sirens without steering his ship onto the rocks. Economists have adopted the episode as the emblem of what they call a commitment device: an arrangement by which a person deliberately restricts their own future options, or makes some of those options more costly, in order to protect a long-term goal from a short-term impulse. The idea sits awkwardly with the traditional model of economic choice, in which a rational agent can only be made worse off by having fewer alternatives. Why would anyone pay, in money or in freedom, to remove choices they could simply decline to make?
B

The standard answer in behavioural economics appeals to what is known as present bias. People, it is argued, do not discount the future at a steady rate; they place disproportionate weight on the immediate moment, so that a reward available now looms far larger than the same reward available tomorrow, while the difference between two distant dates barely registers. One consequence is a systematic gap between plans and actions. On Sunday evening, a week of early nights and healthy lunches seems plainly preferable; by Wednesday, the person who must actually forgo the late film or the pastry sees matters differently. A commitment device is a way of letting the Sunday self overrule the Wednesday self.
C

The empirical literature contains some striking demonstrations. In one widely cited type of study, savers are offered accounts from which they cannot withdraw money before a date or a target of their own choosing, and which pay no more interest than an ordinary account. A substantial minority accept, and those who do tend to accumulate more than comparable savers without such restrictions. Similar designs have been applied to exercise, smoking and study habits, typically by asking participants to deposit a sum that they forfeit if they fail to meet a goal. Online services now allow anyone to do the same, sometimes directing forfeited stakes to a cause the user dislikes, on the reasoning that the prospect of funding one's opponents is especially motivating.
D

It is tempting to read such results as a vindication of the whole programme, and enthusiasts have not always resisted the temptation. Yet the most telling finding in this literature may be the one that receives the least attention: in study after study, the great majority of people offered a commitment device decline it. One interpretation, favoured by the more optimistic, is that most people are naive about their own present bias and therefore fail to see the need for protection. This may be true of some. But it is at least as plausible that many people are accurately weighing the value of flexibility. The future is uncertain; an illness, a family emergency or simply a better opportunity may make yesterday's plan a poor guide to today's interests, and a device rigid enough to defeat temptation will usually be rigid enough to defeat good sense as well.
E

Nor is the evidence on those who do take up commitment uniformly encouraging. A recurrent pattern is that a proportion of participants choose stakes or deadlines that prove too demanding, fail to meet them, and end up worse off than if they had never committed at all. The people most attracted to strict commitment, moreover, appear to be disproportionately those who already struggle with self-control, which is to say precisely those whose predictions about their future behaviour are least reliable. Such individuals may be sophisticated enough to recognise that they have a problem but not sophisticated enough to gauge its size. A tool designed to correct one bias, in short, can be undermined by another.
F

These complications matter more as commitment devices move from the laboratory into institutional design. Several governments and employers have enrolled people automatically in pension schemes from which they may opt out, and some have experimented with plans in which employees commit in advance to direct a share of future pay rises into savings. Such schemes have generally been judged successful on their own terms, increasing participation and contributions. They are not, strictly speaking, commitment devices in Ulysses' sense, since nothing prevents the individual from reversing the choice; their power lies in inertia rather than in constraint. The distinction is not a pedantic one. A default that can be undone at little cost preserves the flexibility whose value the voluntary studies reveal, while a binding commitment imposed or strongly encouraged by an institution transfers the risk of error from the designer to the person bound.
G

Defenders of the paternalistic use of such tools, sometimes called libertarian paternalists, argue that because some default must exist, it may as well be one that serves people's considered interests. The argument has force when the default is genuinely easy to reverse. It has much less when the reversal is made deliberately laborious, as with subscription services that may be joined with a single click but cancelled only by telephone during office hours. The vocabulary of commitment can thus lend a flattering gloss to arrangements whose real beneficiary is the provider. Distinguishing a device that helps people keep their own promises from one that profits from their inattention is not always easy, but it is the distinction on which the legitimacy of the whole approach depends.
H

None of this means that the Ulysses story has been misapplied, only that it has usually been retold without its most instructive detail. Ulysses did not bind himself in ignorance: he knew the precise nature of the danger, its location and its duration, and he instructed his crew to ignore his pleas only for as long as the ship was within earshot of the Sirens. Few of the temptations of ordinary life are so well charted. The lesson of the episode may be less that we should bind ourselves than that we should do so only when we understand the threat about as well as he did.

title: Islands on the Mainland
paras: A

Few ideas in ecology have travelled as far from their point of origin as the equilibrium theory of island biogeography. Formulated in the 1960s by Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson, it was intended to answer a question that had preoccupied naturalists since the great voyages of the nineteenth century: why do some islands support so many more species than others? Their answer was disarmingly economical. The number of species on an island, they argued, reflects not the island's history so much as a dynamic balance between two opposing processes: the arrival of new species from a mainland source, and the local extinction of those already present. When the two rates are equal, species richness settles at an equilibrium, even though the identity of the species making up that total may continue to change.
B

What gave the model its explanatory reach was the way it tied each process to a simple geographical variable. Immigration, MacArthur and Wilson reasoned, should decline with an island's distance from the mainland, since fewer seeds, spores and dispersing animals survive a longer crossing. Extinction should decline with an island's area, because larger islands hold larger populations, and larger populations are less likely to be wiped out by a single disease outbreak or a run of poor breeding seasons. Small, remote islands should therefore be poorest in species, and large islands close to the coast the richest. Field data from archipelagos in the Pacific and the Caribbean appeared broadly consistent with these predictions, and the theory was quickly taken up in textbooks.
C

It was in conservation, however, that the theory found its most consequential, and most contested, application. By the 1970s ecologists had begun to observe that nature reserves on the continents were themselves becoming islands of a kind: patches of forest or grassland stranded in a sea of farmland, roads and towns. If the theory held, such reserves should be expected to lose species over time until they reached a new, lower equilibrium appropriate to their reduced size, a process some writers termed 'relaxation'. Several design principles were derived from this reasoning and were for a time presented almost as rules: reserves should be as large as possible, close to one another, and connected by corridors of habitat along which animals could move.
D

The most celebrated of these prescriptions concerned size and number. Since the theory predicts that a large area will hold more species than a small one, it seemed to follow that one large reserve was preferable to several small ones of the same combined area. This inference provoked a debate, known by its acronym SLOSS ('single large or several small'), that occupied journals for much of the following decade. Critics pointed out that the theory says nothing about which species are present, only how many, and that several small reserves scattered across different habitats might well capture a greater variety of species than one large block confined to a single habitat. They also noted that a single reserve, however large, could be devastated by one fire or epidemic, whereas a population divided among several sites would be less exposed to such a catastrophe.
E

In retrospect, many ecologists regard the SLOSS debate as having generated more heat than light, chiefly because the question was posed at a level of generality that the evidence could not resolve. The answer, it gradually became clear, depended on the species concerned: large predators that range over vast territories plainly require extensive continuous habitat, while many plants and invertebrates can persist indefinitely in modest patches. What the controversy did accomplish was to expose an assumption that had been carried, largely unexamined, from oceanic islands to terrestrial reserves.
F

That assumption concerned the nature of the surrounding 'sea'. For a beetle on a Pacific atoll, the ocean is a genuinely hostile and almost impassable barrier. The farmland, plantations and gardens surrounding a forest fragment are something else entirely. Some species cross them with ease; others use them as a source of food; others still are unable to venture even a few metres beyond the forest edge. Researchers working in this tradition refer to the land between fragments as the 'matrix', and a substantial body of field studies now suggests that the quality of the matrix can matter as much as the size or isolation of the fragments themselves. A reserve surrounded by a mosaic of hedgerows and low-intensity agriculture may behave very differently from one of identical area bordered by intensively sprayed cropland.
G

This shift in emphasis has practical consequences. If fragments are not true islands, conservation need not focus exclusively on enlarging and linking protected areas, an expensive undertaking in densely settled regions. It may be at least as effective to make working landscapes more hospitable, for example by retaining scattered trees in pasture or reducing the use of pesticides near reserve boundaries. Advocates of this so-called 'countryside' approach argue that the long-standing division between land set aside for nature and land given over to production is, ecologically speaking, a false one.
H

None of this means that the original theory has been discarded. Its central insight, that species richness reflects a balance between colonisation and loss, remains a valuable framework, and the relationship between area and species number is among the most consistently observed patterns in ecology. What has changed is the confidence with which the theory is applied. Where it was once treated as a source of design rules, it is now more commonly regarded as a null model: a baseline against which the particular features of a real landscape, such as its matrix, its history and the requirements of its inhabitants, can be measured.

title: What Did Print Change?
paras: A

It has long been a commonplace that the introduction of movable-type printing to Europe in the mid-fifteenth century was one of the hinges on which modern history turns. The Protestant Reformation, the rise of experimental science and the emergence of national vernacular literatures have all, at one time or another, been laid at the door of the press. Yet the more closely historians have examined the period, the less agreement there has been about what, precisely, printing changed, how quickly it did so, and whether the technology should be credited with effects that may have had quite other causes. Part of the difficulty is that the surviving evidence is itself shaped by the technology under investigation: printed books have come down to us in far greater numbers than manuscripts, and historians who work from what happens to survive may overestimate how swiftly the new medium displaced the old. The history of the press has thus become, in part, a history of arguments about the press.
B

The most ambitious claims were advanced in the second half of the twentieth century by scholars who treated printing as an agent of change in its own right. On this view, which the historian Helena Marsh has called 'the revolution thesis', the decisive novelty of print was not speed but fixity. A manuscript copied by hand accumulated errors with each transcription, so that texts tended to degrade as they circulated. Printed editions, by contrast, could be produced in hundreds of identical copies, allowing scholars in different cities to refer to the same page, compare the same tables and correct the same mistakes in subsequent editions. Knowledge, in other words, became cumulative in a way it had not been before, and the intellectual transformations of the following two centuries were, in large measure, its consequence.
C

Critics have challenged this account on several fronts. The first concerns fixity itself. Tobias Wren, whose studies of early printing houses drew on surviving proof sheets and correspondence, found that variation between copies of the same edition was far more common than the revolution thesis supposed. Corrections were frequently made while a press run was under way, so that early and late sheets differed; pirated editions reproduced and multiplied errors; and readers had little means of knowing which copy, if any, was authoritative. For Wren, the reliability that later generations attributed to print was not a property of the technology but a hard-won social achievement, secured gradually through the reputations of particular printers, the policing of guilds and, eventually, legal protections for authors and publishers.
D

A second line of criticism questions the chronology. Agnes Kovač, surveying the output of presses in central Europe, pointed out that for several decades after printing arrived, the books most commonly produced were not new works of scholarship but devotional texts, calendars and school grammars, much as had been copied by hand before. Printers were businessmen operating on narrow margins, and they tended to reproduce what was known to sell. Works by living authors, on her reading of the surviving catalogues, made up only a modest share of output for much of this period. If print eventually fostered intellectual novelty, Kovač argued, it did so only after an extended period in which it had chiefly made familiar material cheaper, and any account that collapses that interval risks attributing to the technology developments that belong to a later age.
E

Nor, it has been argued, was the manuscript world as static as the revolution thesis implied. Daniel Okafor has drawn attention to the commercial scriptoria of late medieval towns, where teams of copyists produced multiple copies of university textbooks by dividing exemplars into sections and copying them simultaneously. Such workshops, he suggests, had already created something resembling a market in standardised texts before Gutenberg's invention. Hand copying, moreover, persisted for centuries alongside print, particularly for material that was politically sensitive, intended for a restricted circle, or simply too specialised to justify the cost of setting type.
F

Defenders of the original thesis have not been without replies. They accept that early printed copies varied but insist that the variation was of a different order of magnitude from that of manuscripts, and that the possibility of standardisation mattered even where it was imperfectly realised. They concede, too, that printers were commercially cautious, but note that even the cheap reproduction of familiar works changed who could own books and how readers related to them. Many now prefer to speak of print as a necessary rather than a sufficient condition of the changes once attributed to it: an enabling technology whose effects depended on the institutions, markets and religious conflicts into which it was introduced.
G

What is perhaps most striking about this debate is how far it has moved from the question with which it began. Few historians would now ask simply whether printing caused the Reformation or the scientific revolution. The more productive questions have proved to be narrower ones: how particular printers established trust, how readers annotated and shared their copies, why some regions adopted the press rapidly and others hesitated. In this respect the historiography of print has followed a familiar trajectory, from a single bold hypothesis to a more crowded and qualified picture in which the technology appears less as a cause than as one participant among many. That outcome need not be read as a defeat for the original thesis, which, whatever its excesses, set the agenda for much of the research that has since complicated it.

title: The Expert Brain and Its Interpreters
paras: A

Few findings in cognitive neuroscience have been reported with as much enthusiasm as those concerning the brains of experts. Studies of taxi drivers, chess masters, musicians and radiologists have repeatedly found that years of specialised practice are associated with measurable differences in brain structure and activity, and these results have been eagerly translated into advice about how the rest of us might acquire similar abilities. I do not wish to dispute the findings themselves, many of which are robust. My concern is rather with the inferences that have been drawn from them, which seem to me to run considerably ahead of what the evidence can support.
B

Consider first the problem of direction. When a group of experts is found to differ from a group of novices in, say, the volume of a particular region of grey matter, it is tempting to conclude that practice produced the difference. But cross-sectional comparisons of this kind cannot by themselves exclude the possibility that people who already possessed the difference were more likely to persist in the activity, perhaps because they found it easier or more rewarding from the outset. The handful of longitudinal studies that have followed individuals before and after training are more informative, and some do suggest that training induces structural change. Even here, however, those who drop out of demanding training programmes are seldom a random sample, and the brains of those who remain may tell us as much about who stays as about what staying does.
C

A second difficulty concerns what is meant by efficiency. A frequently reported finding is that experts show less overall activation than novices when performing a task in their domain, and this is routinely described as evidence that the expert brain works more economically. The interpretation is not unreasonable, but it is far from the only one available. Reduced activation might equally reflect a shift in strategy, the expert retrieving a stored solution rather than computing a fresh one, or the recruitment of a smaller but more specialised network whose contribution is simply harder to detect with current imaging methods. To call the expert brain 'efficient' is to borrow a term from engineering that carries an evaluative charge the data do not, on their own, justify.
D

None of this would matter greatly were it not for the eagerness with which such findings are carried beyond the laboratory. A familiar line of reasoning runs as follows: experts' brains differ from those of novices; the differences are produced by practice; therefore sufficient practice will make anyone an expert. Each step in this chain is weaker than it first appears, and the conclusion, in particular, does not follow even if the premises are granted. That practice is necessary for high performance tells us nothing about whether it is sufficient, still less about whether the same quantity of practice will yield the same benefit for every learner. The research psychologist Miriam Castell has suggested that much popular writing on the subject confuses a description of how experts differ with a prescription for how to become one, and I think she is right to do so.
E

It would be unfair, though, to lay the blame entirely at the door of popularisers. Researchers themselves have sometimes encouraged the more expansive readings, whether through the framing of press releases or through the understandable pressure to emphasise the practical relevance of their work to those who fund it. Nor is the problem one of dishonesty. Neuroimaging studies are expensive, samples are often small, and a striking image of a brain region 'lighting up' is far more communicable than the statistical caveats that ought to accompany it. The result is an asymmetry in which confident claims travel faster and further than the qualifications attached to them.
F

What, then, can legitimately be concluded? I would suggest that the neuroscience of expertise is most valuable not when it purports to explain why experts excel, but when it constrains the range of plausible psychological explanations. If, for example, a theory of chess skill predicts that masters rely on rapid recognition of familiar patterns rather than on deeper calculation, imaging data showing heightened activity in regions associated with object recognition lend that theory some support, and data showing the reverse would count against it. Used in this way, brain measurements become one source of evidence among several, to be weighed alongside behavioural experiments and the detailed study of how experts actually perform, rather than a privileged window onto the underlying truth.
G

There is a further, more general lesson. The appeal of neuroscientific explanation seems to rest partly on an intuition that an account framed in terms of the brain is somehow more fundamental, and therefore more authoritative, than one framed in terms of knowledge, habit or attention. Yet an explanation is not made deeper merely by being relocated to a different level of description. That a radiologist detects a tumour more quickly than a trainee is, in the first instance, a fact about what she has learned to look for; to say that this learning is realised in her visual cortex is true, but it does not by itself make the account any more complete. The brain is, after all, where all learning takes place, and pointing to it explains rather less than it may appear to.
H

I do not conclude from this that imaging research on expertise is misguided. On the contrary, it has already corrected a number of assumptions, including the once common belief that the adult brain is largely fixed in its structure. My argument is only that its findings should be received with the same discipline we would apply to any other body of evidence: with attention to how the data were gathered, to the alternative explanations they leave open, and to the distance between what was observed and what is being claimed.

groups.instr:
Questions 27-31
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
Write
YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

items.q: Much of the research comparing the brains of experts and novices has produced reliable results.
items.why: Đoạn A: 'I do not wish to dispute the findings themselves, many of which are robust'. 'robust' = đáng tin cậy, vững chắc. Tác giả chỉ phản đối các suy luận, không phản đối kết quả -> YES.

items.q: Longitudinal studies provide no more useful evidence than cross-sectional comparisons.
items.why: Đoạn B: 'The handful of longitudinal studies ... are more informative'. Tác giả nói nghiên cứu dọc cho nhiều thông tin hơn, trái với câu hỏi -> NO. Bẫy: tác giả vẫn nêu hạn chế của chúng ('Even here, however...') nên dễ chọn YES.

items.q: Researchers should stop describing expert brains as efficient until better imaging methods become available.
items.why: Đoạn C: tác giả cho rằng từ 'efficient' mang sắc thái đánh giá mà dữ liệu 'do not, on their own, justify' và có nhắc 'current imaging methods'. Nhưng ông không đề xuất ngừng dùng từ này cho đến khi có phương pháp tốt hơn -> NOT GIVEN. Bẫy: đoạn có đủ các chữ 'efficient' và 'imaging methods'.

items.q: Miriam Castell's criticism of popular writing on expertise is justified.
items.why: Đoạn D: sau khi nêu ý của Castell, tác giả viết 'and I think she is right to do so'. Tác giả đồng ý -> YES.

items.q: Researchers who exaggerate the practical value of their findings are usually acting in bad faith.
items.why: Đoạn E: tác giả thừa nhận nhà nghiên cứu đôi khi khuyến khích cách hiểu rộng, nhưng khẳng định 'Nor is the problem one of dishonesty' và nói đến áp lực 'understandable'. 'bad faith' = không trung thực -> NO.

groups.instr:
Questions 32-35
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.q: What is the main purpose of paragraph C?
o: to show that experts use less brain activity because they have learned better strategies
to argue that an observation has been given a label it does not clearly deserve
to explain why current imaging methods cannot detect specialised networks
to suggest that engineers understand efficiency better than neuroscientists
items.why: Đoạn C nêu phát hiện 'less overall activation' bị gọi là 'efficient', rồi đưa ra các cách giải thích khác và kết luận từ này 'carries an evaluative charge the data do not, on their own, justify'. Mục đích: cho thấy một quan sát bị gán nhãn chưa chắc xứng đáng -> B. A chỉ là một trong các khả năng tác giả nêu, không phải kết luận. C và D bóp méo chi tiết phụ.

items.q: In paragraph D, the writer's main objection to the 'familiar line of reasoning' is that
o: experts' brains do not in fact differ from those of novices
practice has been shown to have no effect on the brain
establishing that something is required does not show that it is enough
learners differ too much for any general conclusion to be drawn
items.why: Đoạn D: 'That practice is necessary for high performance tells us nothing about whether it is sufficient'. 'required' = necessary, 'enough' = sufficient -> C. A và B trái với bài (tác giả chấp nhận các tiền đề 'even if the premises are granted'). D dùng ý 'every learner' nhưng tác giả chỉ coi đó là điều chưa được chứng minh, không nói không thể kết luận gì.

items.q: Why does the writer mention the example of chess in paragraph F?
o: to illustrate how brain data can help test a psychological theory
to prove that chess masters rely on pattern recognition
to show that behavioural experiments are more reliable than imaging
to criticise theories of chess skill that ignore calculation
items.why: Đoạn F: dữ liệu hình ảnh não có thể 'lend that theory some support' hoặc 'count against it'. Ví dụ cờ vua minh hoạ cách dữ liệu não giúp kiểm chứng lý thuyết tâm lý -> A. B sai vì tác giả chỉ nói 'some support', không phải chứng minh. C sai vì tác giả coi đây là các nguồn bằng chứng ngang nhau ('one source of evidence among several').

items.q: What point does the writer make with the example of the radiologist in paragraph G?
o: Radiologists' skill depends mainly on the structure of the visual cortex.
Saying where learning happens in the brain does not by itself improve an explanation.
Psychological explanations are more fundamental than neurological ones.
Trainee radiologists should study how the visual cortex works.
items.why: Đoạn G: nói việc học 'is realised in her visual cortex is true, but it does not by itself make the account any more complete'. -> B. C là bẫy: tác giả không nói giải thích tâm lý sâu hơn, chỉ nói giải thích bằng não không tự động sâu hơn ('not made deeper merely by being relocated').

items.why: Đoạn E: 'a striking image of a brain region lighting up is far more communicable than the statistical caveats that ought to accompany it'. Bẫy: 'qualifications' cũng ở đoạn này nhưng đi với 'attached to them', không đi với 'statistical'; câu tóm tắt đã dùng 'warnings' cho ý đó.

items.why: Đoạn F: 'rather than a privileged window onto the underlying truth'. 'view' thay cho 'window'. Phải giữ đúng dạng tính từ 'privileged'.

items.why: Đoạn H: 'corrected ... the once common belief that the adult brain is largely fixed in its structure'. 'overturned' = 'corrected'.

title: Marsden Logistics Staff Handbook
topic: Workplace: annual leave and induction training
paras: A

Annual leave. All full-time employees are entitled to 25 days of paid annual leave per year, in addition to public holidays. Part-time staff receive the same entitlement calculated in proportion to the hours they work. The leave year runs from 1 April to 31 March. After five years of continuous service, employees receive two extra days of leave per year.
B

Requests for leave should be made through the online staff portal at least four weeks in advance for periods of a week or more, and at least three working days in advance for single days. Your line manager will normally respond within five working days. Because the warehouse is especially busy in the run-up to Christmas, leave is not usually granted between 15 November and 24 December, except in exceptional circumstances such as a family emergency.
C

Staff are encouraged to take their full entitlement each year. However, up to five unused days may be carried over into the following leave year, provided they are taken before the end of June. Any remaining days will be lost. If you are unsure how many days you have left, you can check your balance on the portal at any time. Employees who leave the company will be paid for any leave they have earned but not yet taken.
D

Induction training for new staff. All new employees attend a two-day induction programme during their first week. The first day is spent at head office and introduces the company's history, its customers and the main departments. New staff also meet a representative from Human Resources, who explains pay arrangements and the company pension scheme. Lunch is provided on both days, and new staff should bring their bank details and proof of address so that their payroll record can be set up.
E

The second day takes place in the warehouse and focuses on health and safety. Participants are shown how to lift heavy items correctly and are taught the procedure to follow if the fire alarm sounds. Anyone who will drive a forklift truck must also complete a separate three-day course and pass a practical test before operating any vehicle on site. Safety boots are provided free of charge, but staff are responsible for keeping them in good condition.
F

Each new employee is assigned a 'buddy', an experienced colleague from the same team who can answer everyday questions during the first three months. Your buddy is not responsible for assessing your performance; this remains the job of your supervisor. At the end of this probationary period, new staff have a review meeting with their supervisor to discuss their progress and agree on any further training needs. Feedback forms on the induction programme are sent out by email and should be returned within a fortnight.

title: Bees on the Rooftops
paras: A

Walk through the centre of almost any large European or North American city today and there is a good chance that, somewhere above your head, thousands of bees are at work. Urban beekeeping, once regarded as an eccentric pastime, has grown rapidly over the past two decades. Yet the practice is far from new. Until the early twentieth century, it was common for town dwellers to keep a hive or two in a back yard, and honey was an important source of sweetness for families who could not afford sugar. As cities expanded and cheap sugar became widely available, the habit largely disappeared. Its revival began in the 1990s, when a handful of enthusiasts in cities such as Paris and London started placing hives on the roofs of apartment blocks and public buildings.
B

At first glance, a city seems an unlikely home for an insect that depends on flowers. In fact, many beekeepers argue that urban bees are better off than their rural cousins. Modern farmland is often planted with a single crop, which provides a large amount of food for a few weeks and then very little for the rest of the year. Cities, by contrast, offer a remarkable variety of plants in private gardens, parks, cemeteries and along railway lines, and these flower at different times from early spring to late autumn. Urban areas are also generally warmer than the surrounding countryside, which allows bees to start foraging earlier in the year. In addition, gardeners and park managers tend to use fewer chemical pesticides than farmers do.
C

One of the pleasures of city honey is its flavour, which can vary considerably from one neighbourhood to another. Because bees usually collect nectar within about three kilometres of their hive, the honey they produce reflects the plants growing nearby. Honey from an area with many lime trees, for example, has a light, fresh taste, while honey from districts full of private gardens may be darker and more complex. Some beekeepers have taken advantage of this by labelling their jars with the name of the street or district where the hive is located, and customers are often willing to pay extra for honey that comes from their own part of town.
D

Businesses have also become interested. A number of hotels, banks and department stores now keep hives on their roofs, sometimes employing a professional beekeeper to look after them. The honey may be served at breakfast in the hotel restaurant or given to clients as a gift. Managers say that the hives give staff something to talk about and help to demonstrate the company's concern for the environment. Some offices even organise lunchtime visits to the roof, where employees can put on protective suits and watch the bees at close quarters.
E

Experienced beekeepers warn, however, that keeping bees requires much more than good intentions. A colony needs to be inspected about once a week during the warmer months to check that the queen is healthy and that the bees are not preparing to swarm. A swarm, in which around half of the colony leaves the hive to find a new home, can cause alarm when it settles on a car or a shop front in a busy street. Beginners must also be prepared for stings, and for the cost of equipment, which can easily reach several hundred pounds in the first year. For these reasons, most beekeeping associations recommend that newcomers take a course and spend a season helping an experienced keeper before setting up a hive of their own.
F

A more serious concern is the effect of honeybees on other insects. Honeybees are only one of hundreds of bee species, most of which live alone rather than in colonies and receive far less public attention. In some city centres, the number of hives has increased so quickly that there may not be enough flowers to support them all. Researchers in one European capital found that, as the density of hives rose, the number of wild bees visiting flowers in the same area fell. Their conclusion was not that urban beekeeping should stop, but that the number of hives in a district should match the amount of food available.
G

For this reason, many conservationists suggest that people who want to help bees should think beyond the hive. Planting a range of flowering plants, especially native species, provides food for all kinds of pollinating insects. Leaving parts of a lawn uncut until late summer allows wild flowers to grow, and a simple 'bee hotel', made from hollow stems or a block of wood with holes drilled in it, gives solitary bees a place to lay their eggs. These measures cost very little and, unlike keeping a hive, require no special training.

title: Ferry Information and a Fan Heater Guide
paras: A

Westshore Ferries: Passenger Information. Timetable. Ferries run between Port Avon and Carrick Island every day except 25 December. From April to September there are six crossings a day in each direction, with the first ferry leaving Port Avon at 7.15 am. During the winter months the service is reduced to four crossings a day. The journey takes approximately 50 minutes, although it may take longer in rough weather.
B

Tickets. Tickets can be bought online, by phone or at the ticket office at either port. Online bookings receive a 10% discount. Day return tickets are valid only for travel on the date shown. Children under five travel free, and holders of a Senior Rail Card may buy tickets at half price. Vehicle bookings must be made at least 24 hours before departure.
C

Luggage. Foot passengers may bring up to two large bags and one item of hand luggage free of charge. Bicycles are carried for a fee of £4 each way, but space is limited, so cyclists are advised to arrive early. Surfboards and other large sports equipment must be stored in the vehicle deck area.
D

Pets. Dogs are welcome on all crossings but must be kept on a lead at all times. Apart from assistance dogs, they are not permitted in the café or the indoor seating area. A covered pet area with water bowls is available on the upper deck.
E

Breezaire 2 Fan Heater: Getting started. Thank you for buying the Breezaire 2. Before use, remove all packaging and place the heater on a flat, stable surface at least one metre away from curtains, furniture and anything else that could burn. The heater has two heat settings and a cool-air setting for summer use. A built-in thermostat switches the heater off automatically when the room reaches the temperature you have selected.
F

Safety. Never cover the heater or use it to dry clothes. Do not use it in bathrooms or near a swimming pool. If the heater falls over, a safety switch will turn it off immediately. Keep children away from the unit while it is in use, as the front grille becomes hot. Before cleaning, unplug the heater and allow it to cool for at least 30 minutes. Wipe the outside with a dry cloth; do not use water or chemical cleaners.
G

Your guarantee. Your heater is guaranteed for two years from the date of purchase. To extend this to five years, simply register your product on our website within 28 days. The guarantee does not cover damage caused by misuse or by repairs carried out by anyone other than an approved engineer. Please keep your receipt, as you will need it to make a claim.

title: Bayview Hotel: Information for Seasonal Staff
topic: Workplace: staff policies for seasonal hotel workers
paras: A

Shifts and rotas. Seasonal staff work an average of 40 hours a week, spread over five days. Rotas for the following week are published on the staff noticeboard every Thursday. If you wish to swap a shift with a colleague, both of you must sign a shift-change form and have it approved by the duty manager at least 48 hours beforehand. Please check the rota carefully, as shift times can vary from week to week, especially during busy periods such as bank holiday weekends. Overtime is paid at one and a half times your normal hourly rate.
B

Uniform. You will be given three uniform shirts and a name badge on your first day. Housekeeping and kitchen staff also receive non-slip shoes. Uniforms are laundered free of charge on site: simply leave them in the labelled baskets in the staff changing room before 9 am and they will be returned the next day. Lost name badges cost £5 to replace.
C

Accommodation and meals. Staff accommodation is available in shared houses a ten-minute walk from the hotel. Rent of £70 a week is deducted directly from wages. Each house has a fully equipped kitchen, but all staff are also entitled to one free meal per shift in the staff canteen. Guest facilities, such as the swimming pool and gym, may be used by staff only between 2 pm and 4 pm, when they are least busy. Staff are expected to keep shared areas clean and tidy, and a cleaning rota is put up in each house.
D

Training. During your first week you will complete basic food hygiene training, which is compulsory for all staff, whatever their role. Front-of-house staff will also spend a morning shadowing an experienced receptionist to learn the booking system. Staff who wish to gain further qualifications, for instance in first aid, can apply to the training coordinator. The hotel will pay the course fees for anyone who has worked here for at least two months.
E

Sickness and absence. If you are unable to work because of illness, you must telephone the duty manager at least two hours before your shift is due to begin. Text messages and emails are not acceptable. If you are absent for more than three days in a row, you will need to provide a note from a doctor. Repeated absence without a good reason may lead to disciplinary action. Holiday requests should be discussed with your head of department.
F

End of contract. All seasonal contracts end on 30 September. Staff who complete their full contract receive a bonus of £300, paid with their final wages. Anyone who is interested in returning next summer should tell their manager before they leave, as former staff are offered positions before jobs are advertised to the public.

title: Lost and Found
topic: Inside a city lost property office
paras: A

Somewhere beneath a busy railway station, in a long room lined with metal shelves, sit thousands of objects that nobody has come back for. There are umbrellas in every colour, single gloves, school bags, laptops, wedding hats and, on one shelf, a child's wooden rocking horse. This is the lost property office of a large city transport network, and it receives around 250,000 items a year from buses, trains and trams. Its manager, Ruth Calder, has worked there for eleven years and says she is still surprised by what arrives. 'Last spring someone handed in a set of false teeth in a presentation box,' she says. 'They were collected the same afternoon.'
B

Every item follows the same route. When a driver or cleaner finds something, it is placed in a sealed bag with a label showing where and when it was discovered. The bags are delivered to the office overnight, and by the following morning staff have recorded each item on a database, noting its colour, brand and any distinguishing marks. Valuable items such as jewellery, cash and passports are kept in a locked safe, while food and anything else that might go off is thrown away after 48 hours. Passports are not kept for long: if they have not been claimed within a week, they are returned to the embassy of the country that issued them.
C

People who have lost something can fill in an online form describing the item. The database then compares the description with recently recorded objects and suggests possible matches. In the past, this work was done entirely by hand, and staff would spend hours searching through paper records. Calder believes the new system has roughly doubled the number of items returned to their owners, although she admits it is not perfect. 'The computer is good with facts,' she explains, 'but people describe things in very different ways. One person's dark blue coat is another person's black one.' For this reason, a member of staff still checks every suggested match before contacting the owner. When they collect their property, owners must show identification and pay a small fee, which varies according to the type of item.
D

Umbrellas are by far the most common item, especially in autumn, followed by mobile phones, keys and clothing. Phones are now much more likely to be reunited with their owners than in the past, because many people can be identified from the lock screen or contacted through an emergency number stored on the device. Books, on the other hand, are rarely claimed. Calder thinks this is partly because people assume a lost book will never be found and simply buy another copy. Children's toys are a different matter. Parents frequently travel across the city to collect a favourite teddy, and staff make a special effort with these. 'We know a small toy can mean a sleepless night for a whole family,' she says.
E

Items are held for three months. After that, anything unclaimed is either donated or sold. Clothing and blankets go to local homeless shelters, and books are given to schools and hospitals. Electronic devices have all personal data removed before they are sold at regular auctions, along with bicycles, musical instruments and other valuable goods. The money raised helps to cover the cost of running the office, which employs fourteen full-time staff. Some objects never leave. A small collection of unusual finds, including a ship's wheel and a set of Victorian dentist's tools, is kept on display in the staff room.
F

For Calder, the most rewarding part of the job is seeing people reunited with things that matter to them. Many of the most emotional reunions involve objects of little financial value: a letter, a photograph, a grandmother's scarf. She recalls an elderly man who came in to collect a battered leather wallet. It contained only a few coins, but also a photograph of his late wife that he had carried for forty years. 'He shook my hand for about five minutes,' she says. 'That's the kind of thing that makes the job worthwhile.'
G

Calder's advice to travellers is simple. Put your name and an email address or phone number inside bags, cases and even umbrellas, and take photographs of valuable items so that you can describe them accurately if they go missing. Above all, she says, report a loss as soon as possible. 'The sooner we know what we're looking for, the better our chances. People often wait a week before contacting us because they hope the item will turn up at home, and by then the trail has gone cold.'

title: Home Contents Cover and the Wenbury Riverside Festival
topic: Insurance terms and a local festival programme
paras: A

Harwell Home Contents Cover: policy summary. What is covered. This policy protects the contents of your home against loss or damage caused by fire, flood, storm, theft and escape of water. 'Contents' means household goods and personal belongings that you own or are legally responsible for and that are kept inside the home. Items kept in a garage or garden shed are covered up to £1,500 in total, but theft from any outbuilding is covered only where there are visible signs of forced entry.
B

Valuables. No single item is covered for more than £2,000 unless it is named on your schedule. Jewellery, watches and cameras worth over £1,000 must be listed individually, and in the event of a claim you must be able to supply either a receipt or a professional valuation dated within the last three years.
C

Excess and claims. The standard excess (the part of any claim you pay yourself) is £150, rising to £350 for claims involving escape of water, such as a burst pipe or a leaking washing machine. Theft must be reported to the police within 48 hours and to us within seven days. Claims notified more than 30 days after the incident will be declined, except where you can show that you were in hospital or outside the country during that period.
D

Other conditions. If your home is left unoccupied for more than 45 consecutive days, cover for theft and escape of water is suspended until you return. Accidental damage, such as spilling paint on a carpet, is not included as standard; it may be added at any point during the policy year, but cover does not begin until 14 days after it is added. The belongings of lodgers are not covered, although those of family members who live with you permanently are.
E

Wenbury Riverside Festival: programme notes. Lantern Parade (Friday, 7 pm). The parade sets off from the Old Bridge and ends in the Market Square. Free, no booking needed; children under 12 must be accompanied by an adult. In high winds, the parade will be replaced by an indoor lantern display in the Corn Exchange. A decision will be posted on the festival website by 4 pm on the day.
F

Storytelling Tent (Saturday and Sunday, 10 am-4 pm). Free, but each session is limited to 40 places. Tickets are issued at the information point on the day and cannot be reserved beforehand. Sessions are aimed at children aged five to nine, and adults may attend only with a child, with one exception: Sunday's final session at 3 pm is for over-18s only.
G

Riverside Food Market (Saturday only, 11 am-6 pm). Entry costs £3, which is returned as a voucher that can be spent at any stall. Under-16s enter free. Please note that cash is not accepted at the entrance, although most traders inside will take it.
H

Open-air Concert (Saturday, 8 pm, Abbey Meadow). Tickets cost £18 if bought before the festival and £22 on the gate. Festival Pass holders are admitted at no extra charge but must collect a wristband from the box office by 6 pm on Saturday. The concert will go ahead in rain. Folding chairs are not permitted; rugs are welcome. Only if a lightning warning is issued will the event be cancelled, in which case refunds will be made within 30 days.
I

Charity Boat Races (Sunday, from 10 am). Spectators are welcome free of charge along the towpath. Teams of four must register by the Wednesday before the festival; after this, a new team can join only if a registered team withdraws. Rowers must be at least 14, and those aged 14 or 15 must bring a consent form signed by a parent or guardian.

items.q: A bicycle stolen from a locked garage is covered even if the thief left no sign of how they got in.
items.why: Đoạn A: "theft from any outbuilding is covered only where there are visible signs of forced entry". Garage là outbuilding, nên nếu không có dấu vết phá khóa thì không được bồi thường. Bẫy: chữ "locked" làm người đọc nghĩ là đủ điều kiện, nhưng văn bản không nói khóa là đủ.

items.why: Đoạn B: "Jewellery, watches and cameras worth over £1,000 must be listed individually". £1,200 lớn hơn £1,000. Bẫy: con số £2,000 ở câu trước là mức tối đa cho một món chưa liệt kê, không phải ngưỡng bắt buộc liệt kê đồng hồ.

items.why: Đoạn C: excess chuẩn là £150, "rising to £350 for claims involving escape of water, such as ... a leaking washing machine". Excess là phần tự trả, nên rò nước từ máy giặt thì tự trả nhiều hơn so với mất trộm (£150). Câu hỏi diễn đạt lại "excess" thành "pay more of the cost themselves".

items.why: Đoạn E: "In high winds, the parade will be replaced by an indoor lantern display". Bẫy: đoạn H cũng nói về thời tiết, nhưng concert "will go ahead in rain" và chỉ bị hủy khi có cảnh báo sét, không có phương án thay thế.

items.q: The admission charge can be used to buy something at the event.
items.why: Đoạn G: "Entry costs £3, which is returned as a voucher that can be spent at any stall." Tiền vào cửa được đổi thành phiếu mua hàng.

items.q: Buying a ticket in advance is cheaper than paying on arrival.
items.why: Đoạn H: "£18 if bought before the festival and £22 on the gate". Bẫy: đoạn F cũng nói về vé nhưng vé miễn phí và "cannot be reserved beforehand".

items.q: Late applicants can take part only if someone else drops out.
items.why: Đoạn I: sau hạn đăng ký, "a new team can join only if a registered team withdraws". "Drops out" = "withdraws".

items.q: One part of the event is closed to children.
items.why: Đoạn F: "Sunday's final session at 3 pm is for over-18s only". Bẫy: đoạn E có quy định về trẻ dưới 12 tuổi nhưng chỉ yêu cầu có người lớn đi kèm, không cấm trẻ em.

items.q: Some participants need written permission from an adult.
items.why: Đoạn I: người chèo 14 hoặc 15 tuổi "must bring a consent form signed by a parent or guardian". Bẫy: đoạn E chỉ yêu cầu trẻ em có người lớn đi cùng, không phải giấy đồng ý có chữ ký.

items.q: People who have already paid for access must take an extra step before a certain time.
items.why: Đoạn H: "Festival Pass holders ... must collect a wristband from the box office by 6 pm on Saturday." Người đã có Festival Pass (đã trả tiền) phải đi lấy vòng tay trước 6 giờ tối. Bẫy: đoạn E có mốc 4 pm nhưng đó là giờ ban tổ chức thông báo, người tham gia không phải làm gì.

title: Flexible Working and Professional Development at Ashcombe Logistics
paras: A

Flexible Working Policy. Eligibility. Any employee who has completed 26 weeks of continuous service may submit a formal request to change their hours, times or place of work. Agency workers and contractors fall outside this policy. Only one formal request may be made in any twelve-month period, although a request that is withdrawn before a decision is reached does not count towards this limit.
B

Making a request. Requests must be submitted in writing to your line manager, setting out the change you are seeking, the date from which you would like it to take effect and how you believe any impact on your team could be managed. You are not required to give a reason for your request. However, requests connected with caring responsibilities or a medical condition will be given priority where several requests within the same team cannot all be granted.
C

Decisions. Your manager will meet you within 21 days of receiving the request and must notify you of the outcome in writing within two months. A request may be refused only on one of the business grounds listed in Appendix 2, such as an inability to reorganise work among existing staff. Where a request is approved, the change will normally apply for a three-month trial period, after which either party may ask for it to be reviewed. If no review is requested, the arrangement becomes permanent.
D

Remote working. Staff whose roles can be carried out away from the office may work from home for up to three days a week. Employees in warehouse, driving and reception roles are excluded because their duties require them to be on site. Everyone working remotely must attend the office on Tuesdays, the company's team day, unless they have their manager's written agreement to an alternative day.
E

Appeals. If your request is refused, you may appeal to the HR Business Partner for your division within 14 days of receiving the written decision. Appeals are considered by a manager who was not involved in the original decision.
F

Professional Development Scheme. Funding. Permanent employees may apply for funding towards courses and qualifications that are relevant to their current role or to a role they could reasonably move into within the company. The scheme meets the full cost of approved courses up to £2,500 per year; above this figure, the company pays half of any additional cost, up to an overall annual limit of £4,000 per employee. Fixed-term staff with contracts of at least twelve months may apply for short courses costing no more than £500.
G

Study leave. Employees on approved courses receive up to five days of paid study leave per year to attend examinations and to prepare for them. Time spent attending evening or weekend classes is not paid, and cannot be taken as time off in lieu.
H

Repayment. Anyone who resigns within twelve months of finishing a funded course must repay the full cost to the company; this falls to 50% for those who leave between twelve and twenty-four months after completion. Repayment is not required where an employee is made redundant, or where they fail a course despite having attended all sessions.
I

How to apply. Applications are made through the Learning Portal and must be supported by your line manager before they reach the Learning Team. Applications for courses that begin in September must be received by 30 June; those for courses starting at other times of year should arrive at least eight weeks before the start date.

groups.instr: Read the Flexible Working Policy, sections A-E. Do the following statements agree with the information given in the text? Write TRUE if the statement agrees with the information, FALSE if the statement contradicts the information, NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this.

items.q: An employee who withdrew a request in March may make another formal request in May of the same year.
items.why: Đoạn A: mỗi 12 tháng chỉ được một yêu cầu, "although a request that is withdrawn before a decision is reached does not count towards this limit". Yêu cầu đã rút không tính, nên vẫn được nộp yêu cầu mới. Bẫy: người đọc chỉ nhớ quy tắc "one request in any twelve-month period" sẽ chọn FALSE.

items.q: Staff must explain why they want to change their working pattern.
items.why: Đoạn B: "You are not required to give a reason for your request." Bẫy: câu tiếp theo nói yêu cầu liên quan đến chăm sóc người thân hay bệnh tật được ưu tiên, dễ khiến người đọc nghĩ phải nêu lý do.

items.q: Managers are obliged to grant any request made for medical reasons.
items.why: Đoạn B chỉ nói yêu cầu vì lý do sức khỏe "will be given priority where several requests within the same team cannot all be granted". Được ưu tiên khi phải chọn giữa nhiều yêu cầu, chứ không phải bắt buộc chấp thuận. Đoạn C còn nói yêu cầu có thể bị từ chối vì lý do kinh doanh, nên câu này mâu thuẫn với văn bản.

items.q: An approved change continues indefinitely unless someone asks for it to be looked at again after the trial.
items.why: Đoạn C: "If no review is requested, the arrangement becomes permanent." "Continues indefinitely" là cách diễn đạt khác của "becomes permanent".

items.q: A receptionist may work from home one day a week with the manager's agreement.
items.why: Đoạn D: nhân viên lễ tân "are excluded because their duties require them to be on site". Bẫy: cụm "manager's written agreement" trong đoạn chỉ áp dụng cho việc đổi ngày lên văn phòng, không phải cho lễ tân làm ở nhà.

items.q: The HR Business Partner personally decides the outcome of each appeal.
items.why: Đoạn E chỉ nói đơn kháng nghị được gửi tới HR Business Partner và được xem xét bởi "a manager who was not involved in the original decision". Văn bản không cho biết HR Business Partner có phải là người quyết định hay không, cũng không nói người đó là manager hay không, nên không đủ thông tin.

groups.instr: Complete the sentences below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the text for each answer.

items.q: Staff on contracts that are fixed-term must have a contract lasting at least ___ to apply for funding.
items.why: Đoạn F: "Fixed-term staff with contracts of at least twelve months may apply for short courses". Bẫy: con số £500 là giới hạn chi phí khóa học, không phải điều kiện về thời hạn hợp đồng.

items.q: Paid study leave can be used both to sit and to prepare for ___.
items.why: Đoạn G: "paid study leave ... to attend examinations and to prepare for them". "Sit" một kỳ thi = dự thi.

items.q: No pay is given for time spent at classes held in the evening or at the ___.
items.why: Đoạn G: "Time spent attending evening or weekend classes is not paid". Bẫy: câu trước nói về "paid study leave", nhưng ngày nghỉ có lương chỉ dùng cho thi và ôn thi, không dùng cho lớp học buổi tối hay cuối tuần.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.q: An employee takes an approved course costing £3,500. How much will the company pay?
items.why: Đoạn F: công ty trả toàn bộ đến £2,500, phần vượt thì trả một nửa. Phần vượt là £1,000, công ty trả £500, tổng cộng £3,000 (vẫn dưới mức trần £4,000). Bẫy: £4,000 là mức trần năm, £2,500 là mức trả đủ.

items.q: In which situation would an employee NOT have to repay any course fees?
o: They resign eighteen months after completing the course.
They are made redundant six months after completing the course.
They fail the course after missing several sessions.
They resign eleven months after completing the course.
items.why: Đoạn H: "Repayment is not required where an employee is made redundant". A: nghỉ sau 18 tháng vẫn phải trả 50%. C: trượt nhưng không đi học đầy đủ thì không được miễn (điều kiện là "despite having attended all sessions"). D: nghỉ việc trong vòng 12 tháng sau khi học xong thì phải trả toàn bộ.

items.q: An application for a course starting on 1 November must reach the company by
o: 30 June.
1 September.
6 September.
1 October.
items.why: Đoạn I: khóa học không bắt đầu vào tháng Chín phải nộp "at least eight weeks before the start date". Tám tuần trước ngày 1/11 là ngày 6/9. Bẫy: 30/6 chỉ áp dụng cho khóa bắt đầu tháng Chín.

items.q: Before an application reaches the Learning Team, it must be
o: approved by HR.
endorsed by the applicant's manager.
submitted on paper.
accompanied by a course receipt.
items.why: Đoạn I: đơn "must be supported by your line manager before they reach the Learning Team". "Endorsed" = "supported". Bẫy: HR xuất hiện ở phần kháng nghị (đoạn E), không liên quan đến đơn xin tài trợ.

title: The Unmaking and Remaking of Repair
topic: Consumer culture and the revival of repair
paras: A

For most of human history, repairing a broken object was not a hobby, a political statement or a lifestyle choice; it was simply what one did. A cracked pot was riveted, a torn coat was patched, and a clock that had stopped was taken to someone who understood its mechanism. The value of an object lay partly in its capacity to be kept going, and the skills required to keep it going were distributed widely across households and neighbourhoods. What is striking, looking back, is not that people mended things, but how rapidly, over the second half of the twentieth century, the expectation that they would do so evaporated in much of the industrialised world.
B

The usual explanation is economic, and it is not wrong so much as incomplete. As manufacturing costs fell and wages rose, the arithmetic of repair shifted decisively: an hour of a technician's time came to cost more than a new toaster, and replacement became the rational choice. Yet the historian Miriam Okafor has argued that price alone cannot account for the speed of the change. In her account, the decisive factor was design. Products were increasingly assembled with glue rather than screws, sealed in casings that could not be opened without being damaged, and built from components that were never sold separately. Repair did not merely become uneconomic; it became, in a physical sense, impossible, and the knowledge that had once sustained it lost the objects on which it could be practised.
C

This loss was cumulative. A skill that is not exercised is not passed on, and a generation that has never seen a radio opened is unlikely to suspect that it could be. Okafor describes this as a kind of 'mechanical illiteracy', in which consumers come to experience the inside of everyday objects as not merely unfamiliar but forbidden. Warning labels, warranties voided by the removal of a single screw and the sheer density of modern electronics have all reinforced the impression that ordinary people have no business tampering with the things they own. Whether this outcome was deliberately engineered or emerged as a by-product of other priorities, such as making devices thinner and cheaper to assemble, remains a matter of dispute.
D

Over the past fifteen years, however, a counter-movement has gathered pace. Volunteer-run repair cafés, in which people bring broken appliances, clothes and bicycles to be fixed alongside them by skilled volunteers, have spread from a handful of European towns to thousands of locations worldwide. Many began as occasional events in community halls or libraries, and their informal atmosphere is part of their appeal: visitors queue with a kettle or a lamp, talk to strangers while they wait, and are expected to hold the screwdriver themselves rather than hand the object over and come back to collect it later. Their organisers are generally careful to describe their purpose as educational rather than charitable: the aim is not to provide a free service but to return a measure of competence and confidence to the visitor. Records kept by one network suggest that around two-thirds of items brought in leave in working order, though such figures are self-reported and the items that people choose to bring are unlikely to be a representative sample of what is thrown away.
E

Alongside this grassroots activity, legislators in several jurisdictions have begun to intervene. So-called right-to-repair measures typically oblige manufacturers to make spare parts available for a fixed number of years after a model is withdrawn from sale, and to supply repair manuals to independent workshops. Supporters see such rules as overdue corrections to a market that had drifted too far towards disposability. Critics, including some engineers, counter that design for repairability can involve genuine trade-offs: a phone that can be opened easily may be harder to make waterproof, and a modular appliance may use more material than a sealed one. The economist Daniel Reyes has cautioned that if these costs are ignored, regulation may produce products that are easier to fix but break more often.
F

It would be naive, then, to treat repair as an unqualified good. Not every object deserves to be kept alive indefinitely; an old refrigerator may consume so much more electricity than a modern one that replacing it is the more responsible choice. Nor is it obvious that most consumers, given the option, will choose to mend rather than replace. Surveys consistently find that people express strong support for repairable products, but purchasing data tell a less flattering story, suggesting that convenience and novelty continue to outweigh stated principles at the point of sale.
G

What the revival of repair does seem to offer, however, is something that the purely economic debate tends to overlook. To open an object and understand, even roughly, how it works is to alter one's relationship with it, and perhaps with the material world more generally. People who have repaired a lamp or a jacket frequently report that they look after their other possessions differently afterwards. If that change in disposition proves durable, its effects may ultimately matter more than the number of toasters rescued from landfill. The question is less whether repair can compete with replacement on price than whether a society can afford to forget how its own things are made.

groups.instr: The reading passage has seven paragraphs, A-G. Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below.
opts: Laws that require manufacturers to keep repair possible, and their hidden costs
How everyday mending disappeared within a few decades
A benefit of repair that cost comparisons fail to capture
Why repaired products tend to be more reliable
How products were made impossible to open, not just expensive to fix
Community workshops that aim to teach rather than simply to fix
The gap between what consumers say and what they buy, and other limits
How lost knowledge made people feel excluded from their own possessions
The proven environmental advantages of repair
A deliberate plan by manufacturers to discourage repair

items.q: Paragraph A
items.why: Đoạn A nói việc sửa đồ từng là điều hiển nhiên, rồi kết lại bằng ý chính: kỳ vọng đó "evaporated" rất nhanh trong nửa sau thế kỷ 20. Tiêu đề "How everyday mending disappeared within a few decades" nói đúng ý "biến mất trong vài thập kỷ".

items.q: Paragraph B
items.why: Đoạn B thừa nhận lý do kinh tế nhưng ý trọng tâm là của Okafor: "the decisive factor was design", đồ dùng bị dán keo, bịt kín, nên sửa trở thành "in a physical sense, impossible". Tiêu đề "How products were made impossible to open, not just expensive to fix" (không thể mở, chứ không chỉ là đắt) khớp đúng. Bẫy: đoạn có nói về giá, nhưng tác giả nói lý do kinh tế "incomplete".

items.q: Paragraph C
items.why: Đoạn C nói kỹ năng không được dùng thì mất đi, và người tiêu dùng cảm thấy bên trong đồ vật là "forbidden", "no business tampering with the things they own". Tiêu đề "How lost knowledge made people feel excluded from their own possessions" khớp. Bẫy: tiêu đề "A deliberate plan by manufacturers to discourage repair" (kế hoạch cố ý của nhà sản xuất) sai vì đoạn nói việc này có cố ý hay không "remains a matter of dispute".

items.q: Paragraph D
items.why: Đoạn D nói về repair café, mục đích "educational rather than charitable", trả lại năng lực cho người đến sửa. Tiêu đề "Community workshops that aim to teach rather than simply to fix" khớp. Bẫy: con số hai phần ba đồ được sửa xong không phải ý chính, và tác giả còn nghi ngờ số liệu đó.

items.q: Paragraph E
items.why: Đoạn E nói về luật right-to-repair bắt buộc cung cấp linh kiện và tài liệu, rồi nêu các đánh đổi (khó chống nước, tốn vật liệu). Tiêu đề "Laws that require manufacturers to keep repair possible, and their hidden costs" bao quát cả hai ý. Bẫy: tiêu đề "Why repaired products tend to be more reliable" nói đồ đã sửa bền hơn, trong khi Reyes cảnh báo điều ngược lại.

items.q: Paragraph F
items.why: Đoạn F nói sửa chữa không phải lúc nào cũng tốt (tủ lạnh cũ tốn điện) và người tiêu dùng nói một đằng, mua một nẻo ("purchasing data tell a less flattering story"). Tiêu đề "The gap between what consumers say and what they buy, and other limits" khớp. Bẫy: tiêu đề "The proven environmental advantages of repair" nói lợi ích môi trường đã được chứng minh, trái với ví dụ tủ lạnh.

items.q: Paragraph G
items.why: Đoạn G nói sửa chữa mang lại thứ mà "the purely economic debate tends to overlook": thay đổi cách con người đối xử với đồ vật. Tiêu đề "A benefit of repair that cost comparisons fail to capture" khớp (lợi ích mà so sánh chi phí bỏ qua).

groups.instr: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in the reading passage? Write YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer, NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

items.q: Falling prices of new goods are sufficient on their own to explain the decline of repair.
items.why: Đoạn B: lời giải thích kinh tế "is not wrong so much as incomplete". Tác giả cho rằng giá cả chưa đủ để giải thích, nên câu này trái với quan điểm tác giả. Bẫy: tác giả có đồng ý giá là một yếu tố ("not wrong"), nhưng "sufficient on their own" thì sai.

items.q: The success rate reported by repair cafés should be treated with some caution.
items.why: Đoạn D: "such figures are self-reported and the items that people choose to bring are unlikely to be a representative sample". Tác giả ngầm cho rằng con số hai phần ba cần được xem xét thận trọng.

items.q: Right-to-repair laws have already reduced the amount of electronic waste produced.
items.why: Đoạn E nói về nội dung luật và tranh luận ủng hộ/phản đối, nhưng không có thông tin hay quan điểm nào của tác giả về việc luật đã làm giảm rác thải điện tử hay chưa.

items.q: Keeping an old appliance in use is always the more environmentally responsible option.
items.why: Đoạn F: "Not every object deserves to be kept alive indefinitely; an old refrigerator may consume so much more electricity than a modern one that replacing it is the more responsible choice." Tác giả phủ nhận chữ "always".

groups.instr: Complete the summary below. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

items.q: According to Okafor, products became hard to repair because they were held together with ___ instead of screws.
items.why: Đoạn B: "Products were increasingly assembled with glue rather than screws". "Instead of" = "rather than".

items.q: Engineers point out that a phone which opens easily may be more difficult to make ___.
items.why: Đoạn E: "a phone that can be opened easily may be harder to make waterproof".
